title: Generating is not discovering: a pre-registered physics judge for AI-proposed superconductors, calibrated on six known superconductors and one negative control
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Data, dated pre-registrations and supplementary tables S1-S7 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22651560
summary: Generative models now propose millions of "stable" crystal structures, and their own referees have shown that stability is not discovery; no public benchmark asks whether a candidate has the physics to do a job. For superconductors the job is twofold: to pair, with a definite gap symmetry, and to become wire. We present a physics judge that answers both from a structure alone (DFT+U, a gated Wannier model, the full rank-4 RPA susceptibility on a $24^3$ mesh, the linearized gap equation, an irreducible-representation classifier, a manufacturability funnel) and measure what it says about what generators propose. With answer keys pre-registered before computing, the judge was calibrated on six known superconductors (Nb, Nb$_3$Sn, MgB$_2$, BaFe$_2$As$_2$, La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$, YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$), recovering the expected class in all six after two dated corrections. On the ruthenium analogue of the iron pnictide, with two runs and their criterion pre-registered the day before, it returns a null verdict at the same physical interaction where iron gives s$\pm$ ($λ_1 \le 0.0007$ versus 0.096; critical U 4.17 versus 0.97 eV); the pre-registered equal-alpha run fails the letter of the criterion, and we declare the resolution in favour of absolute U as post-hoc. The funnel reproduces the industrial map with thresholds fixed before running. Three generation audits follow: a descriptor sweep over 150 Materials Project metals re-finds the canon; 1,248 MatterGen structures yield 0 candidates that are new, stable and carry a pairing motif; mechanism filters over 47,893 compounds, validated by a blind hold-out, re-derive the community's analogies: geometry plus d-count is necessary but not sufficient. Generation re-finds what is known; judgment is the bottleneck. We propose a public benchmark over the eleven lists of AI-proposed superconductor candidates, none of which classifies gap symmetry.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a physics-based judge that evaluates generative crystal-structure proposals for superconductivity by computing pairing gap symmetry and manufacturability from structure alone, and shows that current generators only re-find known materials rather than making genuine discoveries—framing judgment, not generation, as the bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Generative models propose millions of 'stable' crystal structures, but stability does not equal discovery. No public benchmark currently asks whether a proposed candidate has the actual physics required to perform a job. For superconductors this requires answering two questions: whether the material can pair with a definite gap symmetry, and whether it can be made into a usable wire.
AI.method: A physics judge computes verdicts from structure alone using DFT+U, a gated Wannier model, the full rank-4 RPA susceptibility on a 24³ mesh, the linearized gap equation, an irreducible-representation classifier, and a manufacturability funnel. Answer keys were pre-registered before computing. The judge was calibrated on six known superconductors, tested on the ruthenium analogue of an iron pnictide with pre-registered criteria, and applied in three generation audits: a descriptor sweep over 150 Materials Project metals, 1,248 MatterGen structures, and mechanism filters over 47,893 compounds validated by blind hold-out.
AI.result: The judge recovered the expected gap-symmetry class in all six known superconductors after two dated corrections. On the ruthenium analogue it returned a null verdict (λ₁ ≤ 0.0007 vs. 0.096 for iron; critical U 4.17 vs. 0.97 eV). The funnel reproduced the industrial map with thresholds fixed before running. The descriptor sweep re-found the canon; the 1,248 MatterGen structures yielded zero candidates that were new, stable, and carried a pairing motif; mechanism filters re-derived community analogies, showing geometry plus d-count is necessary but not sufficient.
AI.conclusion: Generation merely re-finds what is already known, whereas judgment is the true bottleneck. The authors propose a public benchmark over the eleven lists of AI-proposed superconductor candidates, none of which currently classifies gap symmetry.

title: Quantum interference between vortex- and impurity-bound states boosts thermoelectricity
summary: Thermoelectric effects in superconductors are generally suppressed by the approximate particle-hole symmetry of the quasiparticle spectrum, but can become pronounced near defects that host particle-hole asymmetric bound states. Here, we investigate how the local thermoelectric response is modified when multiple vortices or nonmagnetic impurities are brought into proximity. Using a lattice Bogolioubov-de Gennes approach combined with linear-response tunneling theory, we calculate the spatially resolved density of states and Seebeck coefficient in $s$- and $d$-wave superconductors. We find that the thermoelectric response can be strongly enhanced when spatially extended defect-induced states overlap. For vortices, this enhancement persists beyond the immediate core regions and originates from interference between vortex-bound states. For impurities, the thermoelectric response exhibits a comparable dependence on impurity separation in the $s$- and $d$-wave cases, although the associated spectral reconstruction is considerably more localized in the $s$-wave superconductor. Our results show that the spatial extent and interference of defect-induced quasiparticle states provide a means of controlling local thermoelectricity in inhomogeneous superconductors, with potential relevance for cryogenic thermoelectric sensing and energy conversion.

AI.tldr: This work uses lattice Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations with linear-response tunneling theory to show that local thermoelectricity (Seebeck coefficient) in s- and d-wave superconductors is strongly enhanced when bound states from multiple vortices or nonmagnetic impurities overlap and interfere. The effect is spatially extended and, for vortices, driven by interference of vortex-bound states, while for impurities the thermoelectric dependence on separation is similar for both pairing symmetries despite more localized spectral reconstruction in the s-wave case.
AI.motivation: Thermoelectric effects in superconductors are usually suppressed by the near particle-hole symmetry of the quasiparticle spectrum, but can become significant near defects hosting particle-hole asymmetric bound states. The paper asks how the local thermoelectric response changes when several vortices or nonmagnetic impurities are placed close together, i.e., whether overlapping defect-induced states enhance local thermoelectricity.
AI.method: The authors combine a lattice Bogoliubov-de Gennes approach with linear-response tunneling theory to compute the spatially resolved density of states and Seebeck coefficient in s- and d-wave superconductors. They compare configurations with multiple vortices and multiple nonmagnetic impurities as a function of defect separation and pairing symmetry.
AI.result: The thermoelectric response is strongly enhanced when spatially extended defect-induced states overlap. For vortices, this enhancement extends beyond the immediate core regions and comes from interference between vortex-bound states. For impurities, the thermoelectric response depends comparably on impurity separation in s- and d-wave cases, although the associated spectral reconstruction is significantly more localized in the s-wave superconductor.
AI.conclusion: The spatial extent and interference of defect-induced quasiparticle states offer a route to controlling local thermoelectricity in inhomogeneous superconductors, with possible applications for cryogenic thermoelectric sensing and energy conversion.

title: Dissipative quantum mechanics of Andreev bound states
summary: We propose a microscopic scheme that allows to describe ac Josephson effect in superconducting junctions in terms of dissipative quantum dynamics of subgap Andreev bound states. This approach is particularly useful for highly transparent junctions at subgap bias voltages in which case a non-trivial combination of Landau-Zener tunneling between Andreev levels and their instability due to quasiparticle escape into continuum may play an important role. In the low bias regime, we evaluate the non-equilibrium current-phase relation of superconducting junctions at arbitrary transmissions and identify a sub-Ohmic phase-dependent dissipative contribution to the current controlled by quasiparticle dynamics near the superconducting gap edge.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a microscopic framework describing the ac Josephson effect via dissipative quantum dynamics of subgap Andreev bound states, highlighting Landau-Zener tunneling and quasiparticle escape, and derives a non-equilibrium current-phase relation with a sub-Ohmic dissipative contribution.
AI.motivation: Highly transparent superconducting junctions at subgap bias voltages exhibit nontrivial interplay between Landau-Zener tunneling between Andreev levels and their instability from quasiparticle escape into the continuum, which existing descriptions do not adequately capture.
AI.method: A microscopic scheme treating the ac Josephson effect as dissipative quantum dynamics of subgap Andreev bound states, incorporating Landau-Zener tunneling between Andreev levels, quasiparticle escape into the continuum, and quasiparticle dynamics near the superconducting gap edge.
AI.result: In the low bias regime, the non-equilibrium current-phase relation of superconducting junctions is evaluated at arbitrary transmissions, and a sub-Ohmic phase-dependent dissipative contribution to the current is identified, controlled by quasiparticle dynamics near the gap edge.
AI.conclusion: The proposed microscopic approach captures the ac Josephson effect in highly transparent junctions through dissipative quantum dynamics of Andreev bound states, revealing a sub-Ohmic dissipative current contribution governed by near-gap-edge quasiparticle dynamics.

title: Out-of-equilibrium relaxation dynamics of the superconducting order parameter in CsV$_3$Sb$_5$
summary: The application of a time-varying strain field drives a superconducting order parameter out of equilibrium. How the order parameter relaxes back to equilibrium depends both on the structure of the superconducting gap and on the nature of quasiparticle scattering. We report the discovery of an ultrasonic attenuation peak inside the superconducting state of the kagome superconductor CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. This peak is the natural consequence of the order parameter relaxation time matching the ultrasonic drive frequency near $T_{\rm c}$. From the measured frequency dependence of the peak, we extract a microscopic scattering time of $τ_N = 25$ ps. This timescale is two orders of magnitude longer than the elastic scattering time as determined by resistivity measurements, but is comparable to the inelastic scattering time determined by thermal transport. Within the conventional framework of order-parameter relaxation, this implies that elastic scattering is ineffective at relaxing the superconducting condensate, consistent with a sign-preserving $s$-wave state obeying Anderson's theorem.

AI.tldr: Ultrasonic attenuation peak inside the superconducting state of kagome CsV3Sb5 reveals a microscopic scattering time of 25 ps, two orders of magnitude longer than the elastic scattering time, consistent with a sign-preserving s-wave state.
AI.motivation: The relaxation of a driven superconducting order parameter back to equilibrium encodes information about the structure of the superconducting gap and the nature of quasiparticle scattering, providing a route to probe gap symmetry in unconventional superconductors such as the kagome metal CsV3Sb5.
AI.method: A time-varying strain field (ultrasound) is applied to drive the superconducting order parameter out of equilibrium. An ultrasonic attenuation peak arising from the order-parameter relaxation time matching the drive frequency near Tc is measured, and its frequency dependence is used to extract the microscopic scattering time.
AI.result: An ultrasonic attenuation peak is discovered inside the superconducting state of CsV3Sb5. Its frequency dependence yields a microscopic scattering time tau_N = 25 ps, two orders of magnitude longer than the elastic scattering time from resistivity but comparable to the inelastic scattering time from thermal transport.
AI.conclusion: Within the conventional order-parameter relaxation framework, the long tau_N implies elastic scattering is ineffective at relaxing the superconducting condensate, consistent with a sign-preserving s-wave state obeying Anderson's theorem.

title: A new generation of effective core potentials: Selected heavy 5d and 6p elements
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. To be published in the Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: We expand the correlation-consistent effective core potentials (ccECPs) library by developing semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets by heavy-elements from $5d$ (Hf, Os, Hg) and $6p$ (Tl, Po, At, Rn) blocks. In order to accurately capture scalar relativistic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and electron-electron correlation, we implement a tiered core-valence partitioning strategy across three distinct resolutions. This includes a small 60-core (Hf, Os, Hg) that explicitly correlates subvalence shells, a large 78-core definition for the main-group elements that rigorously accounts for core polarization and relaxation effects in sparse valence environments, and an intermediate 68-core partition for Hg and Tl. This 68-core architecture represents a unique development in the ccECP library, optimizing the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency in a manner unexplored for ligther elements. Optimized against relativistic all-electron CCSD(T) references, the ccECPs deliver outstanding atomic precision, achieving a global average atomic low-lying states deviation of just 0.045 eV. This accuracy translates directly to robust molecular transferability, systematically restricting dissociation energy discrepancies to under 0.03 eV, equilibrium bond lengths to within 0.005 Å. By enforcing a regularized, finite potential at the origin for enhanced numerical stability in stochastic quantum Monte Carlo methods, this library removes a critical methodological bottleneck for predictive many-body simulations of heavy-element systems and materials.

AI.tldr: This work extends the ccECP library with semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets for heavy 5d (Hf, Os, Hg) and 6p (Tl, Po, At, Rn) elements, using tiered core-valence partitions (60-, 68-, 78-core) benchmarked against relativistic all-electron CCSD(T), achieving ~0.045 eV atomic and <0.03 eV molecular accuracy while enabling stable quantum Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: The correlation-consistent effective core potential (ccECP) library lacked accurate, systematically constructed semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets for heavy elements in the 5d and 6p blocks. Capturing scalar relativistic effects, spin-orbit coupling, and electron-electron correlation for these elements is challenging, and existing pseudopotentials suffer from numerical instabilities that bottleneck stochastic quantum Monte Carlo simulations. A dedicated development was needed to balance accuracy and computational efficiency while removing this methodological limitation.
AI.method: The authors developed semi-local pseudopotentials and matching basis sets for Hf, Os, Hg (5d) and Tl, Po, At, Rn (6p). They implemented a tiered core-valence partitioning strategy at three resolutions: a small 60-core (Hf, Os, Hg) explicitly correlating subvalence shells; a large 78-core partition for main-group elements rigorously accounting for core polarization and relaxation in sparse valence environments; and an intermediate 68-core partition for Hg and Tl. The potentials were optimized against relativistic all-electron CCSD(T) reference data, and a regularized, finite potential at the origin was enforced for numerical stability in stochastic quantum Monte Carlo methods.
AI.result: The ccECPs achieved a global average atomic low-lying state deviation of only 0.045 eV. Molecular transferability was strong, with dissociation energy discrepancies systematically kept under 0.03 eV and equilibrium bond lengths within 0.005 Å. The regularized finite-at-origin potential conferred enhanced numerical stability for quantum Monte Carlo methods.
AI.conclusion: The expanded ccECP library provides highly accurate and transferable pseudopotentials for heavy 5d and 6p elements, with the 68-core partition representing a novel development in the library that optimizes the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. By removing a critical numerical stability bottleneck, this library enables predictive many-body simulations of heavy-element systems and materials via stochastic quantum Monte Carlo methods.

title: Thermal Stability of Encapsulated Molecular Structures with Extended OH-Hydrogen-Bond Chains
summary: Using a coarse-grained model, we performed numerical simulations of the dynamics of linear molecular chains adsorbed on a flat substrate (on the surface of an h-BN crystal). It is shown that molecules containing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups in their structure can form stable hydrogen-bond chains OH$\cdots$OH$\cdots$OH. Such chains can be formed by phenol C$_6$H$_5$OH, 4-phenylphenol C$_6$H$_5$--C$_6$H$_4$OH, paracetamol CH$_3$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide C$_6$H$_5$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH molecules. The dissociation of these chains occurs at temperatures above $T_1=190$, 240, 300, and 400K, respectively. Coating such molecular systems with a hexagonal boron nitride sheet (their van der Waals encapsulation) significantly enhances their thermal stability. Such encapsulated molecular structures retain hydrogen-bond chains up to temperatures of $T_2=470$, 800, 880, and 1140K, respectively. The simulations allow us to conclude that h-BN-encapsulated chains of these molecules can be used to create anhydrous proton-exchange membranes capable of operating at high temperatures. The most promising are encapsulated chains of paracetamol and 4-hydroxybenzanilide molecules.

AI.tldr: Coarse-grained simulations show that linear molecules bearing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups form stable OH···OH···OH hydrogen-bond chains on h-BN; van der Waals encapsulation by an h-BN sheet raises their dissociation temperatures dramatically, suggesting use in high-temperature anhydrous proton-exchange membranes.
AI.motivation: Proton-exchange membranes that operate above the boiling point of water require anhydrous proton conduction, which can be provided by hydrogen-bonded chains. Understanding how such chains form, orient on, and thermally survive on a substrate is a prerequisite for designing high-temperature membrane materials.
AI.method: Numerical simulations using a coarse-grained model of the dynamics of linear molecular chains adsorbed on a flat substrate (the surface of an h-BN crystal). Four molecules with benzene rings and hydroxyl groups were examined: phenol, 4-phenylphenol, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide. Thermal stability of the OH···OH···OH chains was probed by measuring dissociation temperatures, both for free adsorbed chains and for chains encapsulated via van der Waals coating with a hexagonal boron nitride sheet.
AI.result: Stable hydrogen-bond chains (OH···OH···OH) form in all four molecules. Dissociation occurs above T1 = 190, 240, 300, and 400 K for phenol, 4-phenylphenol, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide, respectively. Encapsulation by an h-BN sheet strongly enhances thermal stability, with chains persisting up to T2 = 470, 800, 880, and 1140 K for the same sequence of molecules.
AI.conclusion: h-BN-encapsulated hydrogen-bond chains of these molecules are viable candidates for creating anhydrous proton-exchange membranes operating at high temperatures, with encapsulated paracetamol and 4-hydroxybenzanilide chains being the most promising.

title: Moiré Topology in Twisted Structures with Noncollinear Spin-Orbit Coupling
summary: Moiré superlattices provide a powerful platform for flat bands and correlated topological phases, yet most established examples rely on valley-contrasting Berry curvature in hexagonal lattices. Here, we propose a different route to achieve topological moiré minibands based on noncollinear spin orbit coupling in centrosymmetric type II SOC bilayers. Interlayer hybridization opens local pseudogaps and produces sharply localized Berry curvature, which twisting reconstructs into isolated topological minibands without requiring valley degrees of freedom or hexagonal symmetry. We demonstrate this mechanism in tetragonal Dresselhaus-SOC HgI2, where a Lieb-like moiré potential yields topological flat bands. To improve miniband isolation, we develop a physics-informed machine-learning surrogate that identifies stronger SOC as a key design principle and guides the replacement of Hg by Pb. The resulting PbI2 minibands are narrower and better isolated, supporting correlation-driven magnetism and tunable quantum spin Hall and Chern insulating phases, thereby providing an optimized material realization for experimental exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new route to topological moiré minibands via noncollinear spin-orbit coupling in centrosymmetric type II SOC bilayers, demonstrated in tetragonal HgI2 and optimized to PbI2 using a machine-learning surrogate.
AI.motivation: Most established topological moiré platforms rely on valley-contrasting Berry curvature in hexagonal lattices, which restricts the design space of flat bands and correlated topological phases. A mechanism that does not require valley degrees of freedom or hexagonal symmetry is desirable.
AI.method: The authors propose topological moiré minibands based on noncollinear spin-orbit coupling in centrosymmetric type II SOC bilayers, where interlayer hybridization opens local pseudogaps and produces sharply localized Berry curvature that twisting reconstructs into isolated topological minibands. They demonstrate the mechanism in tetragonal Dresselhaus-SOC HgI2, where a Lieb-like moiré potential yields topological flat bands. A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate is then developed to identify stronger SOC as a key design principle and guide the substitution of Hg by Pb.
AI.result: The ML-guided replacement of Hg by Pb yields PbI2 minibands that are narrower and better isolated, supporting correlation-driven magnetism as well as tunable quantum spin Hall and Chern insulating phases.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a valley-free, non-hexagonal route to topological moiré minibands and provides an optimized material realization (PbI2) for experimental exploration.

title: Irrationality Measure Controls Long-Wavelength Charge Fluctuations in Quasiperiodic Systems
summary: Quasiperiodic order is characterized by irrational frequencies whose rational approximability known as irrationality measure defines distinct arithmetic classes. We establish that this arithmetic classification has direct physical consequences for long-wavelength charge fluctuations. In translation-covariant quasiperiodic systems, the infrared scaling of charge fluctuation is governed by the interplay between the irrationality exponent of irrational frequency and the large-harmonic decay of the hull charge profile: the latter determines the available charge weight, while the former controls how efficiently that weight is transferred to the infrared. Consequently, all algebraic irrational frequencies share the same arithmetic scaling, whereas exceptionally well-approximable transcendental frequencies can exhibit strongly enhanced infrared fluctuation scaling. We further prove that occupied states separated from the Fermi level by a gap stable throughout the hull contribute only an analytic infrared background, leaving the nontrivial scaling to near-Fermi states. Our results extend to general translation-covariant multi-frequency quasiperiodic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper links the arithmetic class of irrational frequencies (via irrationality measure) to the infrared scaling of long-wavelength charge fluctuations in translation-covariant quasiperiodic systems.
AI.motivation: Quasiperiodic order is characterized by irrational frequencies, and their rational approximability (irrationality measure) defines distinct arithmetic classes. The work aims to show these arithmetic distinctions have direct physical consequences for long-wavelength charge fluctuations.
AI.method: The authors analyze translation-covariant quasiperiodic systems, examining how the infrared scaling of charge fluctuations is governed by the interplay between the irrationality exponent of the irrational frequency and the large-harmonic decay of the hull charge profile. They also prove a statement about gapped occupied states and extend results to general multi-frequency quasiperiodic systems.
AI.result: The large-harmonic decay of the hull charge profile determines the available charge weight, while the irrationality exponent controls how efficiently this weight is transferred to the infrared. All algebraic irrational frequencies share the same arithmetic scaling, whereas exceptionally well-approximable transcendental frequencies can exhibit strongly enhanced infrared fluctuation scaling. Occupied states separated from the Fermi level by a hull-stable gap contribute only an analytic infrared background.
AI.conclusion: The arithmetic classification of irrational frequencies has direct physical consequences: it dictates the infrared scaling of charge fluctuations in quasiperiodic systems, with nontrivial scaling arising from near-Fermi states and extensions holding for general multi-frequency translation-covariant quasiperiodic systems.

title: Geometric Ginzburg-Landau theory of charge ordering and commensurability
summary: The concept of quantum geometry has recently led to reinvigorated insights in a wide range of fields including physical responses, superconductivity, and optical transitions, with effects most pronounced in systems with nearly flat dispersion. Here, we show that it plays an essential role in charge density wave formation (CDW) -- an important physical phenomenon that is responsible for driving various sharp changes in material transport properties including metal-insulator transitions. We derive an effective Ginzburg-Landau theory including uncharted contributions and, as a highlight, discover a general criterion for both CDW formation and commensurability transitions where underlying electron-phonon interactions manifest purely as electronic quantum geometric enhancements/suppressions. We benchmark our framework in a class of transition-metal dichalcogenides and resolve a longstanding puzzle where well-established purely kinetic CDW criteria fail in describing the correct ordering wavevector. Besides rendering robust criteria and fundamental insights that are immediately relevant to several experimental charge ordering systems, our theory can also be applied directly to other phonon-mediated phases such as superconductivity, and can be used as an important tool to explore the interplay between various such states. More generally, our framework provides a recipe for investigating the role of quantum geometry in phase transitions.

AI.tldr: This work shows that quantum geometry is essential for charge density wave (CDW) formation, deriving a generalized Ginzburg-Landau theory with a universal criterion for CDW and commensurability transitions, and resolving a longstanding failure of kinetic-only criteria in transition-metal dichalcogenides.
AI.motivation: Quantum geometry has recently yielded new insights in responses, superconductivity, and optical transitions, especially in nearly flat-band systems. However, its role in charge density wave formation—a key phenomenon behind transport anomalies like metal-insulator transitions—remains unexplored.
AI.method: The authors derive an effective Ginzburg-Landau theory that includes previously unaccounted contributions from quantum geometry. From this, they establish a general criterion for CDW formation and commensurability transitions, in which electron-phonon interactions are expressed purely as electronic quantum geometric enhancements or suppressions. The framework is benchmarked on a class of transition-metal dichalcogenides.
AI.result: The theory uncovers a general criterion for both CDW formation and commensurability transitions, and resolves a longstanding puzzle in which purely kinetic CDW criteria fail to predict the correct ordering wavevector in transition-metal dichalcogenides.
AI.conclusion: Quantum geometry provides robust criteria and fundamental insights immediately relevant to experimental charge-ordering systems. The framework extends directly to other phonon-mediated phases such as superconductivity, offers a tool to study the interplay between such states, and supplies a general recipe for investigating quantum geometry in phase transitions.

title: Narrow-line magneto-optical trap of titanium atoms
summary: We realize narrow-linewidth magneto-optical traps of $^{46}$Ti, $^{48}$Ti and $^{50}$Ti atoms based on a 1040 nm-wavelength transition, cooling atoms to a minimum temperature in one dimension of $T_z=990(20)$ nK and a three-dimensional temperature of $T_\mathrm{3D}=1.28(7)$ $μ$K. Atoms are pre-cooled in a broad-line magneto-optical trap and then transferred with about 25% efficiency to the narrow-line trap. We operate the narrow-line trap in two stages over 85 ms. First, a single cooling beam, blue-detuned from the narrow-linewidth atomic resonance, optically pumps and traps the atoms on a two-dimensional surface where the Zeeman shift from the applied spherical quadrupole magnetic field brings the light nearly to resonance. Second, four additional beams, counter-propagating in the transverse directions, cool and compress the atoms in all dimensions. The high magnetic moment of the laser cooling state makes the dynamics of the narrow-line titanium trap similar to those of other magnetic atoms. We measure the lifetime of the excited state of the transition to be $τ=8.2(9)$ $μ$s, indicating a transition linewidth of $γ/2π=20(2)$ kHz, and also measure isotope shifts on the narrow-line transition. We use Stern-Gerlach separation on the ultracold Ti gas to measure the $m_J$-distribution in the narrow-line magneto-optical trap, finding over 98% of the atoms in the stretched spin state.

AI.tldr: Narrow-line magneto-optical traps of three titanium isotopes are realized on a 1040 nm transition, reaching sub-microkelvin temperatures.
AI.motivation: Titanium is a promising candidate for ultracold experiments due to its large magnetic moment and availability of isotopes, but narrow-line laser cooling to ultracold temperatures had not been demonstrated for Ti, motivating the development of a narrow-line MOT on a 1040 nm transition.
AI.method: Atoms are pre-cooled in a broad-line MOT and transferred with ~25% efficiency into a narrow-line MOT, operated in two stages over 85 ms: first a single blue-detuned cooling beam optically pumps and traps atoms on a quasi-2D surface where the quadrupole Zeeman shift brings the light near resonance; then four additional transverse counter-propagating beams cool and compress the gas in all dimensions.
AI.result: A minimum 1D temperature of T_z = 990(20) nK and a 3D temperature of 1.28(7) µK are achieved. The excited-state lifetime is measured as τ = 8.2(9) µs, corresponding to a linewidth of γ/2π = 20(2) kHz. Isotope shifts on the narrow-line transition are measured, and Stern-Gerlach separation shows over 98% of atoms occupy the stretched spin state.
AI.conclusion: This work extends narrow-line magneto-optical trapping and sub-microkelvin cooling to titanium isotopes, with dynamics resembling those of other magnetic atoms thanks to the large magnetic moment, and shows strong spin polarization, enabling ultracold Ti experiments.

title: Combinations of measurements that are simultaneous fits of parameters of interest and systematic uncertainties using the BLUE method
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to EPJC
summary: Combining estimates of the same physics parameter obtained from different measurements improves the precision and robustness of the parameter determination. Modern particle physics measurements are often performed using likelihood fits that include the physics parameter(s) of interest together with nuisance parameters representing systematic uncertainties. In high-statistics analyses, typical of many analyses at the Large Hadron Collider, these nuisance parameters can be constrained in the likelihood fits. We describe how the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator method for combinations can be applied to both the estimates of the parameters of interest and the estimates of the nuisance parameters. We show with concrete example combinations that including the nuisance parameters can improve the precision on the parameters of interest. We show with pseudo-experiments that the uncertainty reported by the combination is reliable and that the approximate likelihood combination proposed in a previous publication and implemented in the Convino software reports an underestimated uncertainty. The method is implemented in an open-source software tool, Combiner.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) method for measurement combinations to include nuisance parameters alongside parameters of interest, demonstrating improved precision and reliable uncertainty via pseudo-experiments, and provides an open-source implementation (Combiner).
AI.motivation: Combining estimates of the same physics parameter from different measurements improves precision and robustness. Modern particle physics measurements use likelihood fits with nuisances representing systematic uncertainties, which can be constrained in high-statistics LHC analyses. A method is needed to properly incorporate these constrained nuisances into the combination.
AI.method: Applying the BLUE method for combinations to both the estimates of parameters of interest and the estimates of nuisance parameters, demonstrated with concrete example combinations and validated using pseudo-experiments.
AI.result: Including nuisance parameters can improve the precision on the parameters of interest. Pseudo-experiments show the combination's reported uncertainty is reliable, whereas the approximate likelihood combination from a previous publication (implemented in Convino) reports an underestimated uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The BLUE-based combination incorporating nuisance parameters provides improved precision and reliable uncertainties. The method is implemented in the open-source software tool Combiner.

title: Consensus in Effective Model Inference for Disordered Ising Systems
summary: When independent learners are trained on data from the same disordered system, finite and noisy samples can lead them to different descriptions of the underlying physics. We quantify the reproducibility of such descriptions through consensus, the degree of agreement among independently trained models. In a teacher-student framework on the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model, an ensemble of students each infers a single uniform effective coupling from a finite set of equilibrium configurations drawn from one quenched bond realization. Aggregating the inferred couplings across students and realizations yields the consensus distribution, whose width quantifies the agreement among learners. The variance of this distribution separates exactly into a finite-sampling contribution, bounded below by inverse of Fisher information, and a quenched-disorder contribution. Sum of these two variance is minimized near critical region, so the consensus width has a minimum near the pseudocritical temperature that sharpens with increasing disorder. The two minima arise from different mechanisms: the sampling term inherits the critical peak of the Fisher information, while the disorder term is temperature-independent at leading order and acquires its critical minimum only at fourth order in the disorder strength, through the covariance between the linear and cubic responses to the bond disorder. Because the students fit a uniform coupling to a heterogeneous lattice, the inferred coupling also carries a misspecification bias that survives in the infinite-data limit. This bias displaces the minimum of the mean-squared error above the consensus minimum, so the temperature at which independent learners agree most closely is not the temperature at which their shared answer is most faithful.

AI.tldr: Independent learners trained on finite, noisy data from the same disordered system can converge on different descriptions of its physics. Using a teacher-student setup on the 2D random-bond Ising model, the authors quantify this reproducibility via a consensus distribution whose variance decomposes into a finite-sampling term (bounded below by inverse Fisher information) and a quenched-disorder term. The summed variance is minimized near the critical region, yielding a consensus width minimum close to the pseudocritical temperature; however, a misspecification bias displaces the minimum of the mean-squared error upward, so maximum inter-learner agreement does not coincide with maximum faithfulness.
AI.motivation: When independently trained learners are exposed to data from the same disordered physical system, finite and noisy samples can drive them toward divergent descriptions of the underlying physics. The paper seeks to quantify the reproducibility of such learned descriptions through the notion of consensus, i.e. the degree of agreement among independently trained models, and to distinguish agreement among learners from fidelity of the learned answer.
AI.method: A teacher-student framework is applied to the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model. An ensemble of students each infers a single uniform effective coupling from a finite set of equilibrium configurations drawn from one quenched bond realization. Aggregating the inferred couplings across students and realizations produces the consensus distribution, whose width measures agreement among learners. The authors analytically decompose the variance of this distribution into a finite-sampling contribution, bounded below by the inverse Fisher information, and a quenched-disorder contribution, and they analyze each term's temperature dependence, including a fourth-order-in-disorder covariance between the linear and cubic responses to bond disorder. The misspecification bias from fitting a uniform coupling to a heterogeneous lattice is also characterized in the infinite-data limit.
AI.result: The consensus distribution variance separates exactly into a finite-sampling term and a quenched-disorder term. The sum of the two variances is minimized near the critical region, so the consensus width exhibits a minimum near the pseudocritical temperature that sharpens as disorder increases. The two minima have distinct mechanisms: the sampling term inherits the critical peak of the Fisher information, whereas the disorder term is temperature-independent at leading order and only acquires its critical minimum at fourth order in the disorder strength, via the covariance between the linear and cubic responses to bond disorder. Because students fit a uniform coupling to a heterogeneous lattice, the inferred coupling carries a misspecification bias that survives in the infinite-data limit; this bias displaces the minimum of the mean-squared error above the consensus minimum.
AI.conclusion: The temperature at which independent learners agree most closely is not the temperature at which their shared answer is most faithful. Consensus, reflecting inter-learner agreement, and mean-squared error, reflecting fidelity to the underlying physics, are minimized at different temperatures, with the misspecification bias pushing the error minimum above the consensus minimum.

title: Janus Dipoles: Fundamentals, Realizations, and Emerging Applications
summary: The Janus dipole - featuring orthogonally oriented electric and magnetic dipoles with a 90-degree phase difference - has emerged as a powerful paradigm for wave manipulation. Unlike traditional Huygens dipoles used for directional control, this unique configuration exhibits strongly asymmetric, face-selective near-field behavior while maintaining a quasi-isotropic far-field radiation pattern. These remarkable properties make the Janus dipole an essential platform for directional wave shaping, with wide-ranging applications in on-chip photonics, quantum interactions, and wireless power transfer. This review systematically traces the rapid development of the Janus dipole from its foundational theoretical inception to its diverse implementation platforms across optical, microwave, and acoustic frequencies. In this paper, we explore the governing principles, classify realization strategies into passive Janus dipoles, active Janus dipoles, and advanced near-field coupling control, and highlight emerging frontiers. By bridging foundational electrodynamics with advanced device engineering, this paper serves as an essential reference and roadmap for researchers designing next-generation, highly integrated, and compact wave-manipulation systems.

AI.tldr: This review traces the Janus dipole from its theoretical inception to implementations across optical, microwave, and acoustic regimes, classifying realization strategies and outlining emerging research frontiers.
AI.motivation: The Janus dipole - orthogonally oriented electric and magnetic dipoles with a 90-degree phase difference - offers strongly asymmetric, face-selective near-field behavior while retaining quasi-isotropic far-field radiation, distinguishing it from traditional Huygens dipoles used for directional control. These properties make it attractive for directional wave shaping in on-chip photonics, quantum interactions, and wireless power transfer, motivating a consolidated review as the field rapidly develops.
AI.method: Systematic review approach: tracing the Janus dipole from foundational theory to diverse implementation platforms at optical, microwave, and acoustic frequencies; articulating governing principles; and classifying realization strategies into passive Janus dipoles, active Janus dipoles, and advanced near-field coupling control.
AI.result: The review organizes the rapidly growing body of Janus dipole research into a coherent taxonomy and highlights emerging frontiers, bridging foundational electrodynamics with advanced device engineering.
AI.conclusion: The paper serves as a reference and roadmap for researchers designing next-generation, highly integrated, compact wave-manipulation systems.

title: Selected Coupled Cluster Guided by Selected Configuration Interaction
summary: Coupled Cluster (CC) theory is one of the most popular correlated wavefunction methods, yet the steep computational cost scaling of CC truncated at higher rank limits its application. Modern Selected Configuration Interaction (SCI) methods successfully exploit the sparsity of ground-state wavefunctions in the determinant space, motivating an analogous approach with the exponential CC ansatz. In this work, we introduce Selected Coupled Cluster (SCC), an arbitrary-order sparse CC method that explicitly solves the CC residual equations within a compact amplitude space guided by an SCI wavefunction. SCC optimizes the CC amplitudes in the sparse amplitude space. Using a pilot Just-in-Time (JIT) compiled implementation, we benchmark SCC against SCI, SCI+PT2, standard rank-truncated dense CC (CCSD, CCSDT), and DMRG across various chemical systems. We demonstrate that SCC exhibits fast, monotonic convergence with the SCI variational threshold, outperforming SCI and surpassing SCI+PT2 in the tight-threshold regime. SCC also provides accurate energies for high-dimensional topologies, where DMRG typically converges slowly with bond dimension. SCC thus presents an efficient drop-in enhancement for modern SCI workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Selected Coupled Cluster (SCC), a sparse arbitrary-order CC method that solves CC residual equations in a compact amplitude space guided by an SCI wavefunction, achieving fast monotonic convergence and outperforming SCI and SCI+PT2 in tight-threshold regimes.
AI.motivation: CC theory suffers from steep computational cost scaling at higher truncation ranks, limiting its applicability; meanwhile, modern SCI methods successfully exploit ground-state wavefunction sparsity in determinant space, suggesting an analogous sparse approach could be applied to the exponential CC ansatz.
AI.method: SCC explicitly solves the CC residual equations within a compact amplitude space guided by an SCI wavefunction, optimizing CC amplitudes in that sparse space. The method is implemented with a pilot Just-in-Time (JIT) compiled code and benchmarked against SCI, SCI+PT2, rank-truncated dense CC (CCSD, CCSDT), and DMRG across various chemical systems.
AI.result: SCC exhibits fast, monotonic convergence with the SCI variational threshold, outperforming SCI and surpassing SCI+PT2 in the tight-threshold regime. It also yields accurate energies for high-dimensional topologies where DMRG converges slowly with bond dimension.
AI.conclusion: SCC is an arbitrary-order sparse CC method that offers efficient, accurate performance and serves as a drop-in enhancement for modern SCI workflows.

title: Competing Interlayer Loop Currents and Superconductivity in the Bilayer $t$-$J_\perp$-$V$ Model
summary: The recent discovery of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in pressurized and thin-film bilayer nickelates, featuring a strong interlayer exchange coupling, and their potential similarities with cuprate superconductors, has made this a very active topic in condensed matter physics. In the present paper we study the strongly correlated one-orbital ($d_{x^2-y^2}$) bilayer $t$-$J_\perp$-$V$ model for nickelates, where $V$ denotes the Coulomb interactions, using a controlled large-$N$ expansion at and beyond the mean-field level. Focusing on the out-of-plane spin exchange interaction ($J_\perp$), we find that it triggers both out-of-plane $s$-wave superconductivity and an out-of-plane bond-order phase ($z$-BOP) instability. The $z$-BOP gives rise to a complex $z$-axis hopping dominated by its imaginary component, which drives out-of-plane currents and induces in-plane ones, spontaneously forming on the vertical plaquettes a loop-current state that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Competition between this loop-current phase and superconductivity yields a dome-shaped superconducting region, with optimal superconductivity occurring near the $z$-BOP quantum critical point. The resulting phase diagram features a pure loop-current region, a low-doping coexistence phase, a pure superconducting state at higher doping, and a correlated metallic state.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes a strongly correlated one-orbital bilayer t-J⊥-V model for nickelates using a controlled large-N expansion, showing that interlayer exchange J⊥ drives both out-of-plane s-wave superconductivity and a z-axis bond-order phase (z-BOP) forming a time-reversal-symmetry-breaking loop-current state, whose competition produces a dome-shaped superconducting region peaked near the z-BOP quantum critical point.
AI.motivation: The discovery of high-Tc superconductivity in pressurized and thin-film bilayer nickelates, with strong interlayer exchange coupling and possible cuprate similarities, has made this an active topic. A controlled theoretical treatment of the strongly correlated bilayer physics is needed to understand the interplay between interlayer exchange and superconductivity.
AI.method: The authors study the strongly correlated one-orbital (d_{x^2-y^2}) bilayer t-J⊥-V model for nickelates, where V is the Coulomb interaction, using a controlled large-N expansion at and beyond the mean-field level, focusing on the out-of-plane spin exchange J⊥.
AI.result: J⊥ triggers both out-of-plane s-wave superconductivity and an out-of-plane bond-order phase (z-BOP) instability. The z-BOP produces a complex z-axis hopping dominated by its imaginary component, driving out-of-plane currents and inducing in-plane ones, spontaneously forming a loop-current state on vertical plaquettes that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Competition between the loop-current phase and superconductivity yields a dome-shaped superconducting region, with optimal superconductivity near the z-BOP quantum critical point.
AI.conclusion: The resulting phase diagram features a pure loop-current region, a low-doping coexistence phase, a pure superconducting state at higher doping, and a correlated metallic state. The competition between the loop-current phase and superconductivity, peaked at the z-BOP quantum critical point, organizes the superconducting dome.

title: A Geometrically Parameterized Quasi-Stationary 3D Model for High-Frequency Induction Tube Welding
summary: A three-dimensional multiphysics finite element framework for the simulation of high-frequency induction welding of tubes is presented. The model couples a time-harmonic magnetic scalar potential formulation with a stabilized quasi-stationary advection-diffusion heat transport equation, enabling accurate prediction of electromagnetic and thermal fields under industrial operating conditions. The framework incorporates parameterized geometry generation and semi-automated, physics-tailored mesh construction and is implemented using the open-source tools GetDP and Gmsh. Validation against measurements from a commercial induction welding line for AISI 304 stainless steel tubes demonstrates good agreement with operating data. The validated model is subsequently applied to investigate the influence of impeder material by comparing a conventional FeNiZnV ferrite with the soft magnetic composite Ferrotron 559H for the induction welding of AISI 304 stainless steel tubes.

AI.tldr: A 3D multiphysics finite element framework couples time-harmonic magnetic scalar potential with stabilized advection-diffusion heat transport to simulate high-frequency induction welding of tubes; validated against industrial AISI 304 data, it is applied to compare FeNiZnV ferrite and Ferrotron 559H impeders.
AI.motivation: High-frequency induction welding of tubes involves tightly coupled electromagnetic and thermal phenomena under industrial conditions, requiring a predictive simulation capability. The study is motivated by the need for an accurate multiphysics model and by the practical question of how impeder material selection affects the welding process.
AI.method: A three-dimensional multiphysics finite element framework is developed, coupling a time-harmonic magnetic scalar potential formulation with a stabilized quasi-stationary advection-diffusion heat transport equation. It includes parameterized geometry generation and semi-automated, physics-tailored mesh construction, and is implemented using the open-source tools GetDP and Gmsh.
AI.result: Validation against measurements from a commercial induction welding line for AISI 304 stainless steel tubes demonstrates good agreement with operating data. The validated model then compares a conventional FeNiZnV ferrite impeder with the soft magnetic composite Ferrotron 559H for welding AISI 304 stainless steel tubes.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables accurate prediction of electromagnetic and thermal fields under industrial operating conditions, is validated against real production data, and provides a basis for evaluating impeder material influence in induction tube welding.

title: Dissipation-induced nonlocal phase-coherent transport in a topological superconductor
summary: Nonlocal phase-coherent transport via Majorana bound states, so-called teleportation, requires Coulomb blockade to suppress local Andreev reflection. We show that dissipation can replace the need for Coulomb blockade. We study a Kitaev chain coupled to a Markovian bath and identify a regime where the magnitude of nonlocal conductance contribution reach the local one. In this regime, the lowest-energy subspace is maximally mixed, reminiscent of a directly-grounded nontrivial topological superconductor. Phase coherence is confirmed by Aharonov-Bohm oscillations. Our results establish dissipation as a tool for controlling quantum teleportation in Majorana systems.

AI.tldr: Dissipation can replace Coulomb blockade to enable phase-coherent nonlocal transport (teleportation) via Majorana bound states, achieving nonlocal conductance comparable to local conductance.
AI.motivation: Nonlocal phase-coherent transport via Majorana bound states (teleportation) normally requires Coulomb blockade to suppress local Andreev reflection, which is a stringent constraint. The paper seeks an alternative mechanism to remove this requirement.
AI.method: A Kitaev chain is coupled to a Markovian bath, and the resulting transport is analyzed to identify a regime where the nonlocal conductance contribution matches the local one. Phase coherence is probed via Aharonov-Bohm oscillations, and the nature of the lowest-energy subspace is examined.
AI.result: A regime is found where the nonlocal conductance contribution reaches the magnitude of the local conductance. In this regime the lowest-energy subspace is maximally mixed, resembling a directly-grounded nontrivial topological superconductor, and Aharonov-Bohm oscillations confirm phase coherence.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation is established as a tool for controlling quantum teleportation in Majorana systems, eliminating the need for Coulomb blockade.

title: On the physical origins of switching diversity in Cu-embedded SiO$_x$ memristive devices
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, Supplementary Information included at the end of the same PDF
summary: Resistive switching devices with sub-stoichiometric SiO$_x$ and pancake-like Cu nanoparticles (Cu-PCs) exhibit distinct macroscopic current-voltage characteristics classified as capacitive or gradual (interface-type switching) and abrupt or resistive (filamentary-type switching), motivating an analysis of the microscopic processes underlying this diversity. It is proposed that the device defect landscape is largely shaped by two charged defect types, mobile oxygen vacancies and immobile Cu-related defects, whose distributions jointly govern interfacial and bulk transport. An effective one-dimensional cloud-in-a-cell simulation framework is employed to reproduce the phenomenological picture of both interface-type and filamentary-type switching by incorporating the dominant coupled ionic and electronic processes underlying these mechanisms. The model includes oxygen-vacancy drift-diffusion, Schottky-limited injection at the metal/oxide interfaces, and bulk trap-assisted transport via Poole-Frenkel conduction, with Cu-PCs near the top interface treated effectively. A simulation-based parametric study varying voltage stress, sweep rate, and oxide thickness is used to examine how these factors rebalance voltage partitioning and the spatiotemporal electric field distribution, thereby altering vacancy redistribution and the relative contributions of interface- and bulk-limited conduction. Using representative, physically motivated parameter sets informed by prior device-level studies, the simulations accurately reproduce the characteristic $I$-$V$ signatures of seven different experimentally observed switching responses. Overall, the findings help to link microscopic defect landscapes and transport processes to experimentally measured macroscopic responses within a single, self-consistent modeling framework.

AI.tldr: An effective 1D cloud-in-a-cell simulation framework links microscopic defect landscapes (mobile oxygen vacancies, immobile Cu-related defects) and coupled ionic/electronic transport to seven experimentally observed SiO_x/Cu-nanoparticle resistive-switching I-V signatures, covering both interface-type and filamentary-type switching.
AI.motivation: Sub-stoichiometric SiO_x resistive switching devices with pancake-like Cu nanoparticles show distinct macroscopic I-V behaviors—capacitive/gradual (interface-type) versus abrupt/resistive (filamentary-type)—and the microscopic origin of this diversity is unclear, motivating a unified analysis of the underlying processes.
AI.method: The device defect landscape is modeled via two charged defect types: mobile oxygen vacancies and immobile Cu-related defects. An effective one-dimensional cloud-in-a-cell simulation framework incorporates coupled ionic and electronic processes: oxygen-vacancy drift-diffusion, Schottky-limited injection at metal/oxide interfaces, bulk trap-assisted Poole-Frenkel conduction, and effective treatment of Cu-PCs near the top interface. A parametric study varies voltage stress, sweep rate, and oxide thickness.

Using representative, physically motivated parameter sets informed by prior device-level studies, the simulations accurately reproduce the characteristic I-V signatures of seven different experimentally observed switching responses.
AI.conclusion: The findings link microscopic defect landscapes and transport processes to experimentally measured macroscopic responses within a single, self-consistent modeling framework.

title: Lattice 2-group symmetries: operators, defects, and gauging
summary: We construct and study lattice realizations of finite 2-group symmetries in ${2+1}$d quantum lattice systems with finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces. We focus on two broad classes of 2-groups with 0-form symmetry group $G$ and 1-form symmetry group $A$: split 2-groups with trivial Postnikov class ${[β]\in\mathcal{H}^3(G,A)}$, and central 2-groups with trivial action ${ρ\colon G\to\text{Aut}(A)}$. In both cases, we construct symmetry operators on the full tensor-product Hilbert space that become 2-group symmetry operators when restricted to the topological subspace of the lattice $A$ 1-form symmetry. While the lattice split 2-group symmetry operators are onsite, the lattice central 2-group symmetry operators are not, and can only be made onsite after introducing ancillae. We extensively explore various manifestations of $ρ$ and $[β]$ for these lattice 2-group symmetry operators and demonstrate their agreement with expectations from quantum field theory. These manifestations arise in the transformation of operators carrying symmetry charge, the structure of lattice 2-group symmetry defects, and the dual fusion 2-category symmetries obtained by gauging the lattice 2-group symmetries. We further propose families of local symmetric Hamiltonians for both classes of lattice 2-group symmetries and identify exactly solvable limits lying in phases with spontaneous 2-group symmetry breaking and nontrivial symmetry-enriched topological order. In one such limit, the gauged Hamiltonians are exactly solvable lattice realizations of the corresponding 2-group gauge theories, whose ground-state degeneracies we calculate.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs and studies lattice realizations of finite 2-group symmetries in (2+1)d quantum lattice systems with finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces, focusing on split and central 2-groups, and explores their manifestations, Hamiltonian realizations, and gauged phases.
AI.motivation: While 2-group symmetries are well understood in quantum field theory, their concrete lattice realizations in (2+1)d systems with finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces remain less developed. The authors aim to bridge this gap by explicitly constructing lattice symmetry operators and verifying that their behavior matches QFT expectations.
AI.method: For two classes of 2-groups — split 2-groups (trivial Postnikov class [β]) and central 2-groups (trivial action ρ) — with 0-form symmetry G and 1-form symmetry A, the authors construct symmetry operators on the full tensor-product Hilbert space that reduce to 2-group symmetry operators on the topological subspace of the A 1-form symmetry. They analyze operator transformations, lattice 2-group symmetry defect structure, and dual fusion 2-category symmetries from gauging.
AI.result: Split 2-group symmetry operators are onsite, whereas central 2-group symmetry operators are not onsite and require ancillae to become onsite. The constructions reproduce QFT expectations via symmetry-charge operator transformations, defect structure, and gauged fusion 2-category symmetries. Families of local symmetric Hamiltonians are proposed for both classes.
AI.conclusion: The work provides explicit lattice realizations and exactly solvable limits for 2-group symmetries, covering spontaneous 2-group symmetry breaking and nontrivial symmetry-enriched topological order. In one limit, gauged Hamiltonians realize the corresponding 2-group gauge theories, with ground-state degeneracies computed.

title: Delay-engineered dynamical phases in a programmable non-Markovian spin oscillator
summary: Non-Markovian dynamics offer a new route towards engineering non-equilibrium matter, where memory and feedback act as programmable resources for controlling order in time. Here we report the realization of a non-Markovian spin oscillator in a hot vapour $^{129}$Xe-Cs co-magnetometer with programmable feedback delay and gain. By tuning these parameters, we observe a hierarchy of dynamical phases, including time-crystalline response, nonlinear bifurcations, and frequency-comb formation. The measured spectra and phase boundaries are captured by linear stability analysis of delayed Bloch equations, revealing these phenomena as different manifestations of the same memory-induced instability structure. These results establish time-delayed feedback as a powerful strategy for controlling non-equilibrium phases, enabling quantum sensing, frequency referencing, and synchronization within a single spin-based platform.

AI.tldr: A non-Markovian spin oscillator with programmable feedback delay and gain is realized in a hot-vapor 129Xe-Cs co-magnetometer, revealing tunable time-crystalline response, nonlinear bifurcations, and frequency-comb formation.
AI.motivation: To explore non-Markovian dynamics as a route to engineering non-equilibrium matter, using memory and feedback as programmable resources for controlling temporal order. The goal is to demonstrate controllable non-equilibrium phases within a spin-based platform, with potential for quantum sensing, frequency referencing, and synchronization.
AI.method: A non-Markovian spin oscillator is implemented in a hot vapor 129Xe-Cs co-magnetometer with programmable feedback delay and gain. Tuning these two parameters allows exploration of the dynamical phase diagram. The measured spectra and phase boundaries are interpreted via linear stability analysis of delayed Bloch equations.
AI.result: A hierarchy of dynamical phases is observed as feedback delay and gain are tuned, including time-crystalline response, nonlinear bifurcations, and frequency-comb formation. The measured spectra and phase boundaries agree with linear stability analysis of delayed Bloch equations.
AI.conclusion: The observed phenomena are different manifestations of a single memory-induced instability structure. Time-delayed feedback provides a powerful strategy for controlling non-equilibrium phases, enabling quantum sensing, frequency referencing, and synchronization within a single spin-based platform.

title: Universal sampling of spin systems across quenched disorder
summary: Statistical physics extracts macroscopic laws by averaging over the many microscopic degrees of freedom of a system. Disordered systems demand a second and far harder average, one over the quenched randomness itself. The classic analytical routes, the replica and cavity methods, become uncontrolled outside mean-field or tree-like limits, and conventional numerical algorithms like parallel tempering require expensive, independent equilibration for every disorder realization. In this work, we introduce a universal neural variational framework that amortizes inference across the disorder ensemble, eliminating both the need for per-instance Markov chain equilibration and the cost of retraining instance-specific variational ansatzes. Built on an encoder-decoder Transformer architecture, after training once, it produces an explicit approximation to the Boltzmann distribution given previously unseen disorder realizations without further optimization. We validate this framework on 2D Edwards-Anderson models, and apply it to the random-bond Ising model, successfully capturing the Binder cumulant crossings near the Nishimori multicritical point. These results shift the object of variational inference from the single instance to the disorder ensemble, opening a route to frustrated many-body systems where instance-by-instance computation is prohibitive.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a neural variational framework that amortizes inference across the disorder ensemble, eliminating per-instance equilibration and retraining for disordered systems, validated on 2D Edwards-Anderson and random-bond Ising models.
AI.motivation: Disordered systems require averaging over quenched randomness, but classic analytical methods (replica, cavity) become uncontrolled beyond mean-field/tree-like limits, and numerical methods like parallel tempering need costly independent equilibration for every disorder realization.
AI.method: A universal neural variational framework built on an encoder-decoder Transformer architecture that, after a single training, produces an explicit approximation to the Boltzmann distribution for previously unseen disorder realizations without further optimization.
AI.result: Validated on 2D Edwards-Anderson models and applied to the random-bond Ising model, successfully capturing Binder cumulant crossings near the Nishimori multicritical point.
AI.conclusion: The object of variational inference is shifted from the single instance to the disorder ensemble, opening a route to frustrated many-body systems where instance-by-instance computation is prohibitive.

title: Scattering-robust Imaging of Azimuthal Features with Enhanced Resolution
summary: Imaging through scattering media remains a long-standing challenge in numerous real-world applications, ranging from medical imaging to long-distance sensing. Recently, illumination consisting of a single orbital angular momentum (OAM) mode, which is structured in the azimuthal coordinate, has been shown to provide enhanced resolution for imaging objects with azimuthal features, with the resolution becoming maximum at an optimal OAM value. However, in the presence of scattering, single-mode fields, which are spatially fully coherent, cause the imaging resolution to decrease significantly due to speckle formation. In this work, we employ azimuthally partially coherent fields and experimentally demonstrate imaging of azimuthal features with enhanced resolution in the presence of scattering. We show that lower degree of azimuthal coherence in such illumination leads to increased robustness against scattering while the azimuthal structure of the illumination ensures enhanced resolution. We derive the condition for best imaging resolution, and we report increase of imaging contrast in scattering from about 7% to 50% as the illumination is changed from a single-mode fully coherent field to that of an azimuthal partially coherent field.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates that azimuthally partially coherent illumination, rather than fully coherent single-OAM-mode fields, enables enhanced-resolution imaging of azimuthal features through scattering media.
AI.motivation: Imaging through scattering media is a persistent challenge. Single-OAM-mode illumination improves resolution for azimuthally featured objects, but its full spatial coherence causes severe speckle-induced resolution loss under scattering. A method is needed that retains enhanced azimuthal resolution while resisting scattering degradation.
AI.method: The authors employ azimuthally partially coherent fields (reduced degree of azimuthal coherence) as illumination and experimentally image azimuthal features in the presence of scattering. They derive the condition for optimal imaging resolution and compare performance against a single-mode fully coherent field.
AI.result: Lower azimuthal coherence yields increased robustness against scattering while the azimuthal structure preserves enhanced resolution. Imaging contrast in scattering improves from approximately 7% (fully coherent single-mode) to 50% (azimuthally partially coherent field).
AI.conclusion: Azimuthally partially coherent illumination offers a route to enhanced-resolution imaging of azimuthal features through scattering media, with a derived criterion for best resolution and a substantial contrast gain over fully coherent illumination.

title: Breaking Water at Graphene Defects
summary: Water dissociation at solid surfaces underpins processes ranging from corrosion and catalysis to electrochemistry and photovoltaics. Defects often serve as reactive sites for dissociation, yet how solvation influences water dissociation at such sites remains poorly understood. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials to explore water dissociation at defective graphene-water interfaces. We show that solvation qualitatively changes the reaction mechanism at a graphene single vacancy (SV), opening pathways that are absent for an isolated water molecule. Whereas the gas-phase process proceeds via a single concerted channel, the solvated SV splits water through two competing pathways: a basic route forming SV-H and OH-(aq), and an acidic route forming SV-OH and H3O+(aq). These lower-barrier pathways produce distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene-water adsorption. Accordingly, even a simple carbon vacancy gives rise to unexpectedly rich interfacial chemistry, coupling surface chemistry to interfacial charge and wettability, with implications for carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.

AI.tldr: Machine-learned interatomic potentials reveal that solvation qualitatively changes water dissociation at a graphene single vacancy, enabling two competing low-barrier pathways (basic and acidic) absent in the gas phase, with implications for carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.
AI.motivation: Water dissociation at solid surfaces is central to corrosion, catalysis, electrochemistry, and photovoltaics. Defects commonly act as reactive dissociation sites, but how solvation modulates dissociation at these sites is poorly understood.
AI.method: State-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials were used to simulate water dissociation at defective graphene-water interfaces, specifically at a graphene single vacancy (SV), comparing gas-phase and solvated reaction mechanisms.
AI.result: Solvation qualitatively alters the reaction mechanism: the gas-phase process proceeds via a single concerted channel, whereas the solvated SV splits water through two competing pathways—a basic route forming SV-H and OH-(aq), and an acidic route forming SV-OH and H3O+(aq). These lower-barrier pathways yield distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene-water adsorption.
AI.conclusion: Even a simple carbon vacancy produces unexpectedly rich interfacial chemistry, coupling surface chemistry to interfacial charge and wettability, with implications for carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.

title: Vacancy Order and Physical Properties of a Ternary Compound Fe0.68Pd0.80Te with an α-Fe1+xTe-Type Structure
summary: We report the identification and characterization of a new compound Fe0.68Pd0.80Te with an α-Fe1+xTe prototype structure. Different from the Fe-square net and minor occupancy of interstitial Fe-sites in Fe1+xTe, Fe0.68Pd0.80Te is featured by a Pdsquare net and near 68% occupancy of the corresponding interstitial Fe-sites. Furthermore, noncontact atomic force microscopy and X-ray diffraction provide evidence for the existence of a 3*3*3 Pd-vacancy order in this layered material. A spin-glass ground state below Tg 40 K is identified via magnetic characterization. Electrical transport measurements show that Fe0.68Pd0.80Te is a semiconductor with a very small band gap below 10 meV. It has weak negative magnetoresistance and holelike charge carriers below room temperature. Our results demonstrate its potentials for further exploring various quantum phenomena.

AI.tldr: Fe0.68Pd0.80Te, a new layered compound with an α-Fe1+xTe prototype structure and a Pd-square net, exhibits a 3×3×3 Pd-vacancy order, spin-glass ground state below ~40 K, and narrow-gap semiconducting transport with weak negative magnetoresistance.
AI.motivation: Fe1+xTe is a well-known parent compound for iron-based superconductivity, where excess interstitial Fe and the Fe-square net govern magnetism and electronic behavior. Substituting Pd offers a route to modify the square net and interstitial occupancy, potentially stabilizing new vacancy-ordered phases and novel quantum states.
AI.method: Synthesis and structural characterization of Fe0.68Pd0.80Te, including noncontact atomic force microscopy and X-ray diffraction to probe vacancy ordering. Magnetic characterization was performed to determine the ground state, and electrical transport measurements probed the band gap, magnetoresistance, and charge-carrier type.
AI.result: Fe0.68Pd0.80Te crystallizes in an α-Fe1+xTe-type structure but features a Pd-square net and ~68% occupancy of interstitial Fe-sites. Evidence for a 3×3×3 Pd-vacancy order was obtained. It shows a spin-glass ground state below Tg ≈ 40 K, semiconducting behavior with a band gap below 10 meV, weak negative magnetoresistance, and holelike carriers below room temperature.
AI.conclusion: The distinct Pd-square net, high interstitial Fe occupancy, and Pd-vacancy ordering yield a spin-glass, narrow-gap semiconductor, demonstrating the potential of Fe0.68Pd0.80Te as a platform for exploring various quantum phenomena.

title: Stress-Testing Dynamical and Generative Downscaling Using Subseasonal Extreme Precipitation Forecasts
comment: 36 pages, 12 figures, 6 tables, submitted to JAMES
summary: Coarse spatial resolution limits the ability of subseasonal prediction models to resolve extreme precipitation. Downscaling with either dynamical or deep generative models can overcome this issue, but the comparative performance of these models for extremes across different atmospheric regimes remains poorly understood. In this work, we evaluate the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model against a diffusion-based generative model by downscaling two physically distinct, extreme precipitation events up to lead times of 3 weeks. For a fair comparison with WRF, which can downscale boundary conditions from different driving models without model-specific training, the diffusion model is trained in an unpaired fashion. Both approaches improve upon the raw European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts forecasts, in comparison to fused rain gauge-radar observations in Switzerland (CombiPrecip), but exhibit regime-dependent strengths. WRF achieves the highest probabilistic skill for a multicell, non-stationary event. Conversely, the diffusion model is more consistent across different performance metrics for the two events, outperforming WRF in a more stationary supercell event. These results demonstrate that explicit dynamical modeling can add value for specific precipitation events for subseasonal lead times, and that generative downscaling adds value more broadly in different situations.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks dynamical (WRF) versus diffusion-based generative downscaling of subseasonal extreme precipitation in Switzerland, showing that WRF excels for a non-stationary multicell event while the diffusion model is more robust across events and outperforms WRF for a stationary supercell event.
AI.motivation: Coarse spatial resolution prevents subseasonal prediction models from resolving extreme precipitation. Both dynamical and deep generative downscaling can address this, but their comparative skill for extremes across different atmospheric regimes is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors downscale two physically distinct extreme precipitation events up to 3-week lead times using the WRF model and a diffusion-based generative model. To enable a fair comparison with WRF (which can downscale boundary conditions from various driving models without model-specific training), the diffusion model is trained in an unpaired fashion. Skill is assessed against fused rain gauge-radar observations (CombiPrecip) in Switzerland.
AI.result: Both approaches outperform raw ECMWF forecasts but show regime-dependent strengths. WRF achieves the highest probabilistic skill for a multicell, non-stationary event, whereas the diffusion model is more consistent across metrics and outperforms WRF for a more stationary supercell event.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dynamical modeling can add value for specific precipitation events at subseasonal lead times, while generative downscaling provides more broadly applicable value across different situations.

title: Controlling topology in flux-mismatched Hofstadter bilayers
summary: Stacked two-dimensional materials provide a promising platform for electrically controlling topological electronic states. However, tunneling between layers hybridizes their bands and removes the crossings needed to change topology. We show that this does not always have to be the case. Band crossings and associated Weyl points are topologically enforced in Hofstadter bilayers whose layers experience different magnetic fluxes. When resonant magnetic Bloch multiplets carry unequal Chern numbers, their projected tunneling is topologically obstructed and must vanish at isolated momenta. Sweeping the layer bias through these zeros creates synthetic Weyl monopoles in momentum-bias space that transfer the Chern mismatch. We demonstrate two consequences: a direct transition between insulating Chern phases and a reentrant compensated metal in which Lifshitz transitions bound the metallic window while internal Weyl events reconstruct the band topology. Consequently, the fixed-filling Hall response remains continuous and nonquantized even as integer Chern number is transferred between bands. Berry-flux, TKNN, and interface calculations independently verify the mechanism and its multichannel chiral signature. We outline realizations in Moire and anomalous-Hall heterostructures, establishing flux mismatch as an experimentally accessible route to electrically programmable Chern phases and chiral transport.
