AI.motivation: Accurate calibration of electromagnetic field strength in the THz regime remains challenging because SI-traceable field sensors are scarce, limiting the ability to benchmark and quantitatively link THz transmitter and receiver systems to absolute standards.
AI.method: The THz electric field is extracted from the Autler-Townes (AT) effect of the cesium 17D5/2→18P3/2 Rydberg transition. The strength of AT-split lines is measured as a function of THz detuning from resonance to determine the on-resonant Rabi frequency, which, together with atomic transition dipole moments and fundamental constants, yields the THz electric field. The atomically measured field calibrates the photomixer transmitter field and power, while simultaneous measurements with a commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver calibrate the receiver's current-to-field responsivity and convert its current-noise floor into an absolute noise-equivalent THz electric-field sensitivity.
AI.result: The atomically measured field calibrates the photomixer transmitter field and power. Simultaneous measurements with a commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver calibrate the receiver's current-to-field responsivity and convert its current-noise floor into an absolute noise-equivalent THz electric-field sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Rydberg atomic sensors provide a practical method for SI-traceable calibration and benchmarking of THz transmitter and receiver systems, and for establishing a quantitative link between state-of-the-art and absolute atom-based THz sensors.

title: A Community-Developed Domain Ontology for Magnetic Materials
summary: Magnetic materials play a crucial role in energy-related technologies, mobility, and sensing, but their complex multiscale behaviour and the coexistence of multiple unit systems pose persistent challenges for data exchange and interpretation. This paper presents a domain ontology for magnetic materials, developed within the European Union funded Magnetic Multiscale Modelling Suite (MaMMoS) project and aligned with the Elementary Multiperspective Material Ontology (EMMO). The ontology formalises intrinsic, hysteretic, and microstructural properties across multiple length scales and supports semantic interoperability between simulation tools, databases, and experimental workflows. One key feature of the ontology is its code-based and human-readable structure, enabled through the EMMOntoPy framework, which allows for direct manipulation and versioning without relying on opaque .owl or .ttl files. This facilitates collaborative development and improves transparency. The ontology supports FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles and is openly available for extension by the community. The aim of the MaMMoS project is to foster reproducibility, improve traceability, and promote the adoption of ontology in the magnetism domain. The ontology that has been developed already serves as the foundation for multiple software tools that handle all kinds of magnetic material data.

AI.tldr: A domain ontology for magnetic materials, built in the EU MaMMoS project and aligned with EMMO, formalises intrinsic, hysteretic, and microstructural properties across length scales to enable semantic interoperability among simulations, databases, and experiments.
AI.motivation: Magnetic materials are central to energy, mobility, and sensing technologies, yet their complex multiscale behaviour and the coexistence of multiple unit systems hinder data exchange and interpretation.
AI.method: Developed within the MaMMoS project and aligned with EMMO, the ontology formalises intrinsic, hysteretic, and microstructural properties across multiple length scales. It uses a code-based, human-readable structure via the EMMOntoPy framework, enabling direct manipulation and versioning without opaque .owl or .ttl files.
AI.result: The ontology supports semantic interoperability between simulation tools, databases, and experimental workflows, upholds FAIR principles, is openly available for community extension, and already underpins multiple software tools handling magnetic material data.
AI.conclusion: The MaMMoS ontology fosters reproducibility, traceability, and ontology adoption in the magnetism domain, while enabling collaborative, transparent development.

title: In-plane magnetic field control of anomalous Hall response enabled by magnetic anisotropy engineering
summary: Engineering magnetic anisotropy provides a powerful route to control magnetization orientation and unlock emerging functionalities in opto-spintronic and current-driven devices. Beyond its role in magnetization reversal, the effective anisotropy can strongly influence the magnetotransport response, offering an additional degree of freedom to tune new device functionalities. In this work, we report a magnetotransport study of a ferrimagnetic [Tb/Co]$_{\times 5}$ multilayer grown with a Tb thickness gradient, whose wedge-shaped tilts the uniaxial anisotropy axis slightly away from the film normal. Anomalous Hall resistivity measurements from 80 K to 300 K reveal a spin reorientation transition, while the angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses exposes the crucial role of the tilted anisotropy. A simplified macrospin model reproduces the full angular response across the transition and shows that the observed anomalous Hall effect when the in-plane magnetic field is applied originates from the tilt of the uniaxial anisotropy axis, which supplies a built-in symmetry-breaking mechanism, enabling in-plane field control over the out-of-plane anomalous Hall response, sign included. These findings establish tilted magnetic anisotropy as a promising route toward Hall effect-based sensor applications and highlight Tb/Co multilayers as a versatile platform for anisotropy-engineered spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: A Tb/Co ferrimagnetic multilayer with a Tb thickness gradient exhibits a tilted uniaxial anisotropy that drives a spin reorientation transition and enables in-plane field control of the out-of-plane anomalous Hall response, including its sign.
AI.motivation: Engineering magnetic anisotropy is a powerful means to control magnetization orientation and unlock new opto-spintronic and current-driven device functionalities. The effective anisotropy not only governs magnetization reversal but can also strongly affect magnetotransport, providing an extra degree of freedom for tuning device behavior. This motivates investigating how a deliberately tilted anisotropy axis modifies magnetotransport. In particular, the authors aim to understand how a tilted uniaxial anisotropy influences the anomalous Hall response across a spin reorientation transition.
AI.method: The authors perform a magnetotransport study on a ferrimagnetic [Tb/Co]×5 multilayer grown with a Tb thickness gradient. The wedge-shaped gradient tilts the uniaxial anisotropy axis slightly away from the film normal. Anomalous Hall resistivity is measured from 80 K to 300 K, and the angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses is characterized. A simplified macrospin model is used to reproduce the full angular response across the transition.
AI.result: Anomalous Hall resistivity measurements reveal a spin reorientation transition between 80 K and 300 K. The angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses exposes the crucial role of the tilted anisotropy. The macrospin model reproduces the full angular response across the transition and shows that the observed anomalous Hall effect under an in-plane magnetic field originates from the tilt of the uniaxial anisotropy axis. This tilt supplies a built-in symmetry-breaking mechanism, enabling in-plane field control over the out-of-plane anomalous Hall response, including its sign.
AI.conclusion: Tilted magnetic anisotropy is established as a promising route toward Hall effect-based sensor applications, and Tb/Co multilayers are highlighted as a versatile platform for anisotropy-engineered spintronic devices.

title: Silicon Solar Cell Design for >30% Efficiency via Singlet Fission
summary: Singlet fission (SF) materials convert high-energy photons into multiple charge carriers, providing a route to exceed the efficiency limits of single-junction silicon solar cells without many of the complexities of multi-junction tandem designs. Following the first demonstration of an SF-enhanced silicon solar cell in 2025, there is a need to understand how SF materials can be effectively integrated into high-efficiency industrial silicon devices and translated from proof of concept to a manufacturable technology. Using coupled optical and electrical simulations, we assess the efficiency potential of several industrially relevant silicon cell architectures combined with SF materials. Interdigitated back-contact (IBC) cells offer the greatest potential for improvement due to unrestricted front-surface access and can achieve efficiencies exceeding 33%. However, performance is highly sensitive to front-surface passivation quality. Appropriate silicon design, particularly controlled surface doping and fixed interfacial charge, can mitigate recombination losses and relax passivation requirements for ultra-thin exciton-transfer layers.

AI.tldr: Coupled optical-electrical simulations show that integrating singlet fission (SF) materials with industrially relevant silicon architectures—especially interdigitated back-contact (IBC) cells—can exceed 33% efficiency, though performance hinges critically on front-surface passivation quality.
AI.motivation: SF materials convert high-energy photons into multiple charge carriers, offering a path to surpass single-junction silicon efficiency limits without the complexity of multi-junction tandems. After the first SF-enhanced silicon solar cell was demonstrated in 2025, there is a need to understand how SF materials can be integrated into high-efficiency industrial silicon devices and translated from proof of concept to manufacturable technology.
AI.method: Coupled optical and electrical simulations assessing the efficiency potential of several industrially relevant silicon cell architectures combined with SF materials, examining factors such as front-surface passivation and silicon design (controlled surface doping, fixed interfacial charge).
AI.result: IBC cells offer the greatest improvement potential due to unrestricted front-surface access, achieving efficiencies exceeding 33%. However, performance is highly sensitive to front-surface passivation quality; appropriate silicon design can mitigate recombination losses and relax passivation requirements for ultra-thin exciton-transfer layers.
AI.conclusion: IBC architectures are the most promising route for SF-enhanced industrial silicon cells, and combining suitable silicon design with SF integration can reduce passivation demands, aiding translation toward manufacturable high-efficiency devices.

title: Nondipole Coulomb effects in strong x-ray field ionization
summary: Atomic ionization in superintense x-ray fields is studied through numerical solutions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation including nondipole corrections. The role of the Coulomb potential of the atomic core in the nondipole regime is analyzed for a linearly polarized laser field. In the considered high-frequency and high-intensity stabilization regime, the photoelectron spectra are dominated by a near-zero-energy structure, while above-threshold ionization peaks are suppressed. Two sub-regimes in the nondipole case are identified based on the scaling of the Coulomb momentum transfer, when the Coulomb effect during the interaction with the laser field is either significant or minor. The Coulomb influenced regime sets in within the realm of relatively low field strengths, high laser frequencies, and long pulse durations. An intuitive model explaining the distinct features in the photoelectron momentum distributions and the Coulomb effect scaling is provided.

AI.tldr: Atomic ionization in superintense x-ray fields is studied via the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with nondipole corrections, revealing a near-zero-energy structure in photoelectron spectra and two nondipole sub-regimes governed by Coulomb momentum transfer scaling.
AI.motivation: Superintense x-ray fields probe atomic ionization beyond the dipole approximation, yet the role of the atomic core Coulomb potential in the nondipole regime remains insufficiently understood, particularly in the high-frequency, high-intensity stabilization regime.
AI.method: Numerical solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation including nondipole corrections, applied to a linearly polarized laser field, with analysis of the Coulomb momentum transfer scaling and an intuitive model of the photoelectron momentum distributions.
AI.result: Photoelectron spectra are dominated by a near-zero-energy structure while above-threshold ionization peaks are suppressed. Two nondipole sub-regimes are identified according to the scaling of Coulomb momentum transfer, where the Coulomb effect during laser interaction is either significant or minor. The Coulomb-influenced regime appears at relatively low field strengths, high laser frequencies, and long pulse durations.
AI.conclusion: The atomic core Coulomb potential qualitatively shapes nondipole ionization dynamics in the stabilization regime, and the identified sub-regimes and intuitive model provide a framework for interpreting photoelectron momentum distributions and Coulomb effect scaling in superintense x-ray fields.

title: Rare-History Transitions in Temporally Random Integrable Quantum Circuits
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Supplemental Material will be submitted separately. This is an initial draft, and comments are welcome
summary: We study current fluctuations in a temporally random integrable quantum circuit. Commutativity reduces every drive history exactly to its layer composition, turning annealed fluctuations into a competition between current gain and the large-deviation cost of rare compositions. For each fixed composition, homogeneous thermodynamic Bethe ansatz dressing supplemented by ballistic fluctuation theory yields the conditional current statistics. Their annealed large-deviation contraction predicts a first-order switch between two dominant history classes, terminating on a line of regular cusp endpoints. Finite-time analysis shows how the switch is rounded. Thus temporal randomness can act as an emergent order-parameter-like coordinate in trajectory space.

AI.tldr: Current fluctuations in a temporally random integrable quantum circuit are shown to reduce, via commutativity, to a competition between current gain and the large-deviation cost of layer compositions, producing a first-order switch between dominant history classes.
AI.motivation: Temporal randomness in integrable quantum circuits is generally expected to complicate current statistics; the paper asks how annealed fluctuations behave when the drive is random in time and whether randomness can play a nontrivial organizing role in trajectory space.
AI.method: The authors exploit commutativity to map every drive history exactly onto its layer composition, converting annealed fluctuations into a competition between current gain and the large-deviation cost of rare compositions. For each fixed composition, homogeneous thermodynamic Bethe ansatz dressing combined with ballistic fluctuation theory yields the conditional current statistics; annealed large-deviation contraction then delivers the full distribution, supported by finite-time analysis of the rounding of the transition.
AI.result: The annealed large-deviation contraction predicts a first-order switch between two dominant history classes, terminating on a line of regular cusp endpoints. Finite-time analysis shows how this switch is rounded.
AI.conclusion: Temporal randomness can act as an emergent order-parameter-like coordinate in trajectory space, providing a new organizing principle for current fluctuations in integrable quantum circuits.

title: Fingerprints of Excitonic Collective Modes in the Two-Dimensional Electron Gas
summary: The two-dimensional homogeneous electron gas (2D HEG) is a prototype system of fundamental interest that can be realized experimentally over a wide range of densities. Here, we investigate its collective charge excitations at low densities, using time-dependent density functional theory. We demonstrate that, beyond traditional plasmons, new collective excitonic modes emerge for a Wigner-Seitz radius larger than $r_{\mathrm s} \approx 1$. These excitonic modes leave characteristic fingerprints in experimentally accessible quantities, namely, asymmetric peak structures in the loss function and very strong Friedel-like oscillations in the static linear density response that increase when the system approaches a regime of instability. Indeed, at low enough densities the collective modes cross the zero energy axis, indicating an instability of the paramagnetic 2D HEG towards the formation of a charge-density-wave phase with excitonic origin. These findings provide valuable insights for the experimental detection of excitonic collective modes in tunable 2D electron systems and contribute to the fundamental understanding of many-body effects in low-density electron gases.

AI.tldr: Using time-dependent DFT, the authors predict new collective excitonic modes in the low-density 2D homogeneous electron gas beyond traditional plasmons, with experimental fingerprints and an instability toward a charge-density-wave phase.
AI.motivation: The 2D homogeneous electron gas is a prototype many-body system realizable over a wide density range, and understanding its collective charge excitations at low densities is of fundamental interest, particularly regarding excitonic and instability physics.
AI.method: Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) is applied to compute collective charge excitations, the loss function, and the static linear density response of the 2D HEG at low densities.
AI.result: New collective excitonic modes emerge for Wigner-Seitz radius r_s > ~1, producing asymmetric peaks in the loss function and strong Friedel-like oscillations in the static density response that grow near instability. At sufficiently low densities, collective modes cross the zero-energy axis, signaling an instability toward a charge-density-wave phase of excitonic origin.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer guidance for experimental detection of excitonic collective modes in tunable 2D electron systems and advance understanding of many-body effects in low-density electron gases.

title: U-Shaped Fermi-Level Dependence of Point-Defect Aggregation Enthalpy in Silicon
summary: Point defects govern the electronic and structural behavior of silicon, yet their configuration and energy depend on both the charge state and the Fermi level (EF). Using an unbiased global structure search with first-principles calculations, we screened more than 1,500 candidate structures, covering intrinsic defects and C, H, O, N, P, and B impurities in charge states from -2 to +2. The reaction enthalpy of defect aggregation depends on EF in a U shape, being strongest where the net charge transferred during the reaction vanishes and weaker toward both band edges. This U arises because complexes are more charge-neutral than their isolated constituents, so the net charge transfer changes sign across the gap. The point where this sign change occurs is set by the transition levels of the specific defects. For typical reactions, the driving force is tunable by 0.3-0.5 eV, which shifts the equilibrium complex concentration by five to eight orders of magnitude at room temperature. Our results make the Fermi level a practical lever for defect engineering in as-grown and irradiated silicon.

AI.tldr: Using global structure search and first-principles calculations on 1,500+ candidate defect structures in silicon, this work shows that the reaction enthalpy of defect aggregation follows a U-shaped dependence on the Fermi level, tunable by 0.3-0.5 eV.
AI.motivation: Point defects control the electronic and structural behavior of silicon, but their configuration and energy depend on charge state and Fermi level. A systematic understanding of how the Fermi level governs defect aggregation energetics is needed for defect engineering.
AI.method: Unbiased global structure search combined with first-principles calculations, screening over 1,500 candidate structures including intrinsic defects and C, H, O, N, P, and B impurities in charge states from -2 to +2, analyzing the Fermi-level dependence of defect aggregation reaction enthalpies.
AI.result: The reaction enthalpy of defect aggregation exhibits a U-shaped dependence on the Fermi level, being strongest where net charge transfer vanishes and weaker toward both band edges. This arises because complexes are more charge-neutral than their isolated constituents, causing the net charge transfer to change sign across the gap, with the sign-change point set by the transition levels of the specific defects. The driving force is tunable by 0.3-0.5 eV, shifting equilibrium complex concentration by five to eight orders of magnitude at room temperature.
AI.conclusion: The Fermi level acts as a practical lever for defect engineering in as-grown and irradiated silicon, offering substantial control over defect aggregation and complex concentrations.

title: Topological band structure of excitons in octochlore KTb$_{3}$F$_{10}$: an analog of the Luttinger Semimetal
summary: Understanding the symmetry and topology of band structures in crystalline solids has been among the defining themes of a generation of condensed matter physicists, with implications across many different platforms including electronic bands, photonic crystals, phonons and magnetic excitations. In the latter systems, there is usually magnetic long-range order and time reversal symmetry breaking. Here we further enrich the possible band structures available to magnetic systems by examining dispersive crystal field excitations above a ground state that is a simple product of singlets. In these systems, there is an interplay of magnetic interactions and band topology with both crystal and time reversal symmetries. Using high-resolution neutron spectroscopy we reveal the dispersion relations of bosonic excitons in KTb$_{3}$F$_{10}$, an experimental realization of the octochlore lattice. We show that there are pinch point features in the scattering intensity. The dominant coupling in this system is the long-range magnetostatic dipolar interaction, whose singularity at the zone center is passed onto the scattering intensity. However, the pinch points survive when the range of the dipoles is truncated to finite shell number in the form of a three-band quadratic band touching protected by cubic symmetry. This model, which is related to the Luttinger semi-metal, provides a general long wavelength model for the emergence of pinch point scattering intensity encompassing also the true long-range dipolar model.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates dispersive crystal field excitations above a singlet-product ground state in the magnetic system KTb$_3$F$_{10}$ (an octochlore lattice realization), revealing pinch point features in neutron scattering intensity. The dominant long-range magnetostatic dipolar interaction transfers its zone-center singularity to the scattering intensity, while pinch points persist even when dipole range is truncated to finite shells via a three-band quadratic band touching protected by cubic symmetry.
AI.motivation: The study of symmetry and topology in crystalline band structures has largely focused on systems like electronic bands, photonic crystals, phonons, and magnetic excitations. Magnetic systems typically involve long-range order and time reversal symmetry breaking. The authors aim to enrich the range of possible band structures in magnetic systems by examining dispersive crystal field excitations above a simple singlet-product ground state, where magnetic interactions and band topology interplay with both crystal and time reversal symmetries.
AI.method: High-resolution neutron spectroscopy is used to measure the dispersion relations of bosonic excitons in KTb$_3$F$_{10}$, an experimental realization of the octochlore lattice. The dominant coupling is identified as the long-range magnetostatic dipolar interaction. The authors analyze the singularity at the zone center and its transfer to scattering intensity. They also examine the effect of truncating the dipole range to finite shell number, leading to a three-band quadratic band touching protected by cubic symmetry, related to the Luttinger semi-metal.
AI.result: Pinch point features are observed in the scattering intensity of KTb$_3$F$_{10}$. The singularity at the zone center from the long-range magnetostatic dipolar interaction is passed onto the scattering intensity. Importantly, the pinch points survive when the dipole range is truncated to a finite shell number, manifesting as a three-band quadratic band touching protected by cubic symmetry. This model provides a general long-wavelength description for the emergence of pinch point scattering intensity, encompassing the true long-range dipolar model.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that magnetic systems with singlet-product ground states can host nontrivial band topology, with pinch point scattering intensity arising from both long-range dipolar interactions and a truncated-dipole model featuring a cubic-symmetry-protected three-band quadratic band touching. This enriches the understanding of band structures in magnetic systems and connects to concepts from Luttinger semi-metals.

title: Work as a function of protocol duration for the efficient erasure of an underdamped memory: isothermal to adiabatic transition
summary: We use evolutionary reinforcement learning to determine efficient time-dependent erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever moving in a double-well potential, an experimental realization of a 1-bit memory. We investigate how the mean work $\langle W \rangle $ needed to erase a bit scales as a function of the protocol duration $τ$. We find two regimes, depending on how $τ$ compares to the relaxation time of the system $t_r$. For $τ\gg t_r$, the quasistatic isothermal regime, we recover Landauer's bound plus an overhead that scales as $1/τ$, similar to the overdamped case. By contrast, for $τ<t_r$ erasure becomes adiabatic and $\langle W \rangle$ grows more slowly than in the isothermal case. This growth is bounded from below as $1/τ$, which we derive using a gedanken optimal protocol. Finally, comparison with overdamped erasure shows that learned protocols can outperform protocols that are optimal subject to equilibrium boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: Evolutionary reinforcement learning finds time-dependent erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever in a double-well potential (a 1-bit memory). Mean work scales differently depending on protocol duration τ relative to relaxation time t_r: for τ≫t_r the isothermal regime recovers Landauer's bound plus 1/τ overhead, while for τ<t_r erasure becomes adiabatic with work growing more slowly, bounded below by 1/τ. Learned protocols can outperform those optimal under equilibrium boundary conditions.
AI.motivation: To determine efficient time-dependent erasure protocols and understand how the mean work needed to erase a bit scales with protocol duration in an underdamped system, extending known results beyond the overdamped regime.
AI.method: Evolutionary reinforcement learning is used to design erasure protocols for an underdamped cantilever moving in a double-well potential, an experimental realization of a 1-bit memory. The scaling of mean work with protocol duration is analyzed in two regimes separated by the relaxation time, supported by a gedanken optimal protocol derivation and comparison with overdamped erasure.
AI.result: Two regimes emerge. For τ≫t_r (quasistatic isothermal), Landauer's bound is recovered plus an overhead scaling as 1/τ, similar to the overdamped case. For τ<t_r, erasure becomes adiabatic and mean work grows more slowly than in the isothermal case, bounded from below as 1/τ. Learned protocols can outperform protocols optimal subject to equilibrium boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The scaling of erasure work with protocol duration in the underdamped regime differs qualitatively between the isothermal and adiabatic limits, with a lower bound of 1/τ in the fast (adiabatic) regime. Learning-based protocols can exceed the performance of equilibrium-constrained optimal protocols.

title: Block entropy area based non-local fermionic mode optimization with gradient disentanglers
summary: We introduce a systematic block entropy area based mode optimization algorithm for many-body quantum states of interacting fermions represented by matrix product states. From the gradient of a global cost function, the block entropy area, a long-ranged, non-interacting effective disentangler Hamiltonian is formed. We then simulate the time-dependent Schrödinger equation driven by the disentangler Hamiltonian by employing the time-dependent variational principle based on projector splitting, and minimize the cost function. The combination of the density matrix renormalization group with this gradient-based entanglement minimization forms an efficient low-rank iterative ground-state algorithm that also provides an optimized single-particle basis for matrix product state representation. We demonstrate the method on two-dimensional lattice models of interacting fermions and the Fe${_4}$S${_4}$ cluster, and show its robustness and superiority over earlier protocols using nearest-neighbor mode rotations and reorderings.

AI.tldr: A gradient-based mode optimization algorithm minimizing "block entropy area" via a long-ranged disentangler Hamiltonian, combined with DMRG, yields an efficient low-rank ground-state method with an optimized single-particle basis for interacting-fermion MPS.
AI.motivation: Matrix product state (MPS) representations of interacting fermions suffer from high entanglement and rank when the single-particle basis is suboptimal. Earlier mode-optimization protocols relying on nearest-neighbor orbital rotations and reorderings are limited in reducing entanglement, motivating a more global, systematic optimization.
AI.method: A global cost function, the block entropy area, is defined. Its gradient generates a long-ranged, non-interacting effective disentangler Hamiltonian. The time-dependent Schrödinger equation under this Hamiltonian is simulated using the time-dependent variational principle with projector splitting, iteratively minimizing the cost function. This gradient-based entanglement minimization is combined with the density matrix renormalization group.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on two-dimensional lattice models of interacting fermions and the Fe4S4 cluster, showing robustness and superiority over earlier protocols that used nearest-neighbor mode rotations and reorderings.
AI.conclusion: Combining DMRG with gradient-based entanglement minimization forms an efficient low-rank iterative ground-state algorithm that simultaneously optimizes the single-particle basis for MPS representation, outperforming prior local mode-rotation schemes.

title: Enhancing charge stability of Ge quantum well heterostructures via SiGe layer composition engineering
summary: Composition modulation is a powerful technique for designing materials with tailored properties, fueling the development of advanced semiconductor devices. In this work, we have implemented this technique into Ge quantum well heterostructures, offering a promising avenue to address the critical challenge of charge stability in spin qubit devices. Harnessing the atomic-scale precision of molecular beam epitaxy, we have engineered the band structure of the SiGe top barrier via graded composition modulation, thereby reducing charge accumulation states at the SiGe-dielectric interface and strengthening the effective confinement to the hole gases in the Ge quantum wells. The enhanced charge stability of composition-modulated SiGe/Ge quantum well heterostructures is confirmed in Hall devices, featuring an enlarged stable gate voltage range. We have further fabricated quantum dot devices from the composition-modulated SiGe/Ge quantum well heterostructures and observed remarkably low charge noise with an averaged amplitude of $0.46\,\mathrm{μeV}/\mathrm{\sqrt{Hz}}$ at $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$---the lowest reported value for Ge quantum wells grown on silicon. This exceptional charge stability of the quantum dots persists in the few-hole regime, with no observable voltage drift over $\sim$hours. With reduced charge noise and enhanced energy stability, composition-modulated SiGe/Ge heterostructures exhibit significant potential for applications in building high-performance quantum devices, including spin qubits with a long coherence time.

AI.tldr: Composition modulation of the SiGe top barrier in SiGe/Ge quantum wells is shown to suppress interfacial charge accumulation, yielding record-low charge noise in Ge quantum dots on silicon.
AI.motivation: Charge instability (charge accumulation states and charge noise) at the SiGe-dielectric interface is a critical obstacle for spin qubit devices based on Ge quantum well heterostructures. Composition modulation is introduced as a means to engineer the band structure and thereby improve charge stability.
AI.method: Using the atomic-scale precision of molecular beam epitaxy, the band structure of the SiGe top barrier was engineered via graded composition modulation. This reduces charge accumulation states at the SiGe-dielectric interface and strengthens confinement of the hole gas in the Ge quantum wells. The approach was validated in Hall devices, and quantum dot devices were then fabricated from the composition-modulated heterostructures for noise characterization.
AI.result: Composition-modulated SiGe/Ge heterostructures exhibit an enlarged stable gate voltage range. Quantum dots fabricated from these heterostructures show remarkably low charge noise, with an averaged amplitude of 0.46 μeV/√Hz at 1 Hz—the lowest reported value for Ge quantum wells grown on silicon. This stability persists in the few-hole regime, with no observable voltage drift over ~hours.
AI.conclusion: Composition modulation of the SiGe barrier effectively reduces charge noise and enhances energy stability in SiGe/Ge quantum wells, making these heterostructures promising for high-performance quantum devices such as long-coherence-time spin qubits.

title: High-Performance Scaled P-Type SnOx Transistor by Atomic Layer Deposition with CFET Integration
summary: The development of high-performance p-type oxide semiconductors is essential for realizing complementary logic for monolithic 3D integration, yet p-type oxide semiconductors still exhibit substantially inferior performance compared with their n-type counterparts. In this work, we demonstrate high-performance p-type SnOx transistors by atomic layer deposition (ALD), as back-end-of-line compatible devices for monolithic 3D integration. The SnOx transistors exhibit high field-effect mobility of 6.9 cm2/Vs, low subthreshold swing (SS) of 185 mV/dec, decent on/off ratio (ION/IOFF) of 1.8*104 and high bias stability. By scaling the channel length down to 80 nm, a high on-current of 38.7 mA/mm at VDS of -1 V is achieved. It is understood that precursor and reaction engineering to suppress Sn4+ component in SnOx film are the key for performance enhancement. Furthermore, a complementary field-effect transistor with ALD SnOx p-FET vertically stacking on ALD In2O3 n-FET is also demonstrated, achieving maximum voltage gain of 21 V/V at VDD of 4 V. These findings suggest ALD SnOx as a promising candidate for scaled high-performance BEOL p-type transistors.

AI.tldr: ALD-deposited p-type SnOx transistors achieve high mobility (6.9 cm2/Vs), low SS, and a high on-current (38.7 mA/mm at 80 nm channel), enabling a vertically stacked complementary FET with ALD In2O3 n-FET.
AI.motivation: p-type oxide semiconductors are essential for complementary logic in monolithic 3D integration but lag substantially behind their n-type counterparts, and back-end-of-line (BEOL) compatible high-performance p-type devices are needed.
AI.method: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) of SnOx films with precursor and reaction engineering to suppress the Sn4+ component, fabricating p-FETs and scaling channel length to 80 nm; a complementary FET is built by vertically stacking an ALD SnOx p-FET on an ALD In2O3 n-FET.
AI.result: SnOx transistors show field-effect mobility of 6.9 cm2/Vs, SS of 185 mV/dec, ION/IOFF of 1.8*104, high bias stability, and on-current of 38.7 mA/mm at VDS = -1 V for 80 nm channel; the stacked complementary FET reaches a maximum voltage gain of 21 V/V at VDD = 4 V.
AI.conclusion: Suppressing the Sn4+ component via precursor and reaction engineering is key to performance enhancement, and ALD SnOx is a promising candidate for scaled high-performance BEOL p-type transistors.

title: Robust Spin-1 Haldane Topology under Itinerant Doping
summary: We study itinerant hole doping of the spin-$1$ Haldane symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase in two $t$--$J$ chains coupled by ferromagnetic (FM) Hund exchange. Density-matrix renormalization group calculations show that string order, a finite spin gap, and the Haldane entanglement structure coexist over a broad doping range. Combined with entanglement-entropy scaling consistent with a single gapless charge mode, these results support a metallic doped Haldane SPT with a $C1S0$ low-energy description. At low doping, short-range charge correlations reduce the density of spin-$1/2$ defect rungs, whereas at larger doping their positions become nearly uncorrelated while their spins are collectively incorporated into the correlated spin sector. The doped Haldane SPT terminates in a fully spin-polarized FM phase, which forms a reentrant pocket at high doping in the global phase diagram. Dilute-limit analyses trace the two FM boundaries to spin--charge factorization at weak Hund coupling and to rung-triplet binding with reduced pair mobility at strong Hund coupling. Our results show how mobile carriers reorganize the Haldane spin structure while preserving its characteristic signatures.

AI.tldr: DMRG study of hole doping in a two-chain spin-1 Haldane SPT coupled by ferromagnetic Hund exchange reveals a metallic doped Haldane SPT with a C1S0 low-energy description, terminating in a reentrant fully spin-polarized FM phase.
AI.motivation: The fate of the spin-1 Haldane symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase under itinerant hole doping remains largely unexplored, particularly in multi-chain geometries with magnetic exchange coupling. Understanding whether topological signatures such as string order, spin gap, and Haldane entanglement structure survive carrier doping is key to connecting SPT physics with metallic behavior.
AI.method: Two t-J chains coupled by ferromagnetic (FM) Hund exchange are studied using density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations. Signatures of the Haldane SPT (string order, spin gap, entanglement structure) and entanglement-entropy scaling are analyzed across a broad doping range. Dilute-limit analyses are used to identify the mechanisms governing the FM phase boundaries.
AI.result: String order, a finite spin gap, and the Haldane entanglement structure coexist over a broad doping range, with entanglement-entropy scaling consistent with a single gapless charge mode, supporting a metallic doped Haldane SPT with a C1S0 low-energy description. At low doping, short-range charge correlations reduce the density of spin-1/2 defect rungs; at larger doping their positions become nearly uncorrelated while their spins join the correlated spin sector. The doped Haldane SPT terminates in a fully spin-polarized FM phase forming a reentrant pocket at high doping. The two FM boundaries arise from spin-charge factorization at weak Hund coupling and rung-triplet binding with reduced pair mobility at strong Hund coupling.
AI.conclusion: Mobile charge carriers reorganize the Haldane spin structure while preserving its characteristic topological signatures, yielding a metallic doped Haldane SPT. The global phase diagram features a reentrant fully spin-polarized FM phase, with distinct weak- and strong-Hund-coupling mechanisms setting its boundaries.

title: Certified reduced-basis emulation of conformal field theories on the fuzzy sphere
summary: Fuzzy-sphere regularization gives numerical access to three-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs), but locating one requires testing for criticality across the parameter space of microscopic couplings. We reduce the search cost by about two orders of magnitude, combining an exact diagonalization based on states having definite total angular momentum with a certified reduced-basis emulator that reconstructs energies, observables and their derivatives continuously across the couplings from a handful of exact solutions per system size. The combination reproduces the published ground-state-energy analysis of the fuzzy-sphere Ising model and the published conformal data of a three-flavor fuzzy-sphere realization of the O(2) Wilson--Fisher CFT, including quantities defined by parameter derivatives. Applied to the O(2) model with no CFT input, the ground-state-energy criterion locates the critical coupling to within half a percent of a density matrix renormalization group value obtained on systems more than twice the size, and maps the critical line of the model across the coupling plane. Ground-state criteria locate the critical line robustly, but the point they select along it is weakly determined, and the computed dimensions come closest to the bootstrap elsewhere along the line.

AI.tldr: An exact-diagonalization scheme using total-angular-momentum sectors combined with a certified reduced-basis emulator cuts the cost of locating 3D CFTs on the fuzzy sphere by ~2 orders of magnitude, reproducing published Ising and O(2) Wilson–Fisher results and locating the O(2) critical coupling to within 0.5% of a much larger DMRG value.
AI.motivation: Fuzzy-sphere regularization provides numerical access to 3D CFTs, but finding a critical point requires scanning the microscopic coupling parameter space for criticality, which is computationally expensive. The paper aims to reduce this search cost dramatically.
AI.method: Two ingredients are combined: (1) exact diagonalization restricted to states with definite total angular momentum, and (2) a certified reduced-basis emulator that reconstructs energies, observables, and their parameter derivatives continuously across couplings from only a handful of exact solutions per system size.
AI.result: The approach reproduces the published ground-state-energy analysis of the fuzzy-sphere Ising model and the published conformal data of a three-flavor fuzzy-sphere realization of the O(2) Wilson–Fisher CFT, including derivative-defined quantities. Applied to the O(2) model without CFT input, the ground-state-energy criterion locates the critical coupling within 0.5% of a DMRG value obtained on systems more than twice as large, and maps the critical line across the coupling plane.
AI.conclusion: Ground-state criteria robustly locate the critical line, but the specific point selected along it is weakly determined; the computed scaling dimensions come closest to bootstrap results elsewhere along the line.

title: High-fidelity k$\cdot$p representations of first-principles electronic band structures through covariant renormalization
summary: The k$\cdot$p method can be applied directly to first-principles energies and momentum matrix elements, but the resulting models converge slowly with the number of bands and are inexact wherever the underlying Hamiltonian is nonlocal. We show that both limitations can be largely removed by renormalizing the eigenvalue spectra of the Hermitian momentum matrices. These spectra are gauge invariant, and are identical for symmetry-related Cartesian components, hence scaling the recurring magnitudes provides a modest set of parameters that preserves degeneracies and crystal symmetry without needing to construct a symmetry-adapted basis. We choose to renormalize the models against reference eigenvalues and band velocities on rays out of a high-symmetry point. For GaP, a 15-band model can reproduce the band structure in the near-gap reference regions within a few meV. For zincblende and wurtzite AlN, similar accuracy requires 30- or 66-band models, which in the case of zincblende is traced to the strong warping in the [110] direction. The scheme readily generalizes to rocksalt PbTe, which includes spin-orbit coupling, and has L-centered valence and conduction band extrema. Further, we demonstrate, for GaP, how compact four-band Hamiltonians can be obtained by downfolding within the same renormalization scheme. Moreover, by changing the fitting regime to encompass the entire Brillouin zone, the scheme can be used to generate full-zone models that reproduce the density of states. The practical utility is illustrated with a 59-band k.p model for GaP, which can be evaluated on meshes far denser than the reference calculation, that in turn can be used both to resolve fine features in the density of states and to compute the hole conductivity at low temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a renormalization scheme for k·p models based on the gauge-invariant eigenvalue spectra of Hermitian momentum matrices, which removes the slow convergence with band number and the inaccuracy caused by nonlocal Hamiltonians. Applying the scheme to GaP, AlN (zincblende/wurtzite), and PbTe yields few-meV accuracy in near-gap reference regions with 15-, 30-/66-, and spin-orbit-inclusive models respectively, and enables compact downfolded and full-zone models for density-of-states and transport calculations.
AI.motivation: The conventional k·p method applied directly to first-principles energies and momentum matrix elements suffers from two limitations: the resulting models converge slowly with the number of bands, and they are inexact wherever the underlying Hamiltonian is nonlocal. The authors aim to overcome both limitations to obtain accurate, compact, and symmetry-preserving k·p models.
AI.method: The authors renormalize the eigenvalue spectra of Hermitian momentum matrices, which are gauge invariant and identical for symmetry-related Cartesian components. Scaling the recurring magnitudes yields a modest parameter set that preserves degeneracies and crystal symmetry without constructing a symmetry-adapted basis. Models are fit against reference eigenvalues and band velocities on rays emanating from a high-symmetry point. The scheme is generalized to spin-orbit-coupled systems and to downfolding for compact Hamiltonians, and can also be refit over the entire Brillouin zone to produce full-zone models.
AI.result: For GaP, a 15-band model reproduces the near-gap band structure within a few meV. For zincblende and wurtzite AlN, comparable accuracy requires 30- or 66-band models, with the zincblende case traced to strong warping along [110]. The scheme extends to rocksalt PbTe with spin-orbit coupling and L-centered valence/conduction extrema. Compact four-band Hamiltonians are demonstrated for GaP via downfolding, and a 59-band full-zone GaP model reproduces the density of states and enables hole-conductivity computation at low temperature.
AI.conclusion: Renormalizing the spectra of Hermitian momentum matrices provides a gauge-invariant, symmetry-preserving route to accurate and compact k·p models from first-principles data. The approach handles nonlocal Hamiltonians, generalizes across crystal structures and spin-orbit coupling, supports downfolding to few-band models, and can generate full-zone models useful for resolving fine density-of-states features and computing transport properties on dense meshes.

title: Néel-Vector-Dependent Altermagnetic Spin Splitting in the One-Dimensional Limit
summary: Altermagnetism is normally identified by nonrelativistic spin-split bands in a compensated collinear magnet. Under one-dimensional confinement, however, this diagnostic can disappear: a boundary-compatible sublattice-exchange operation may leave the only Bloch momentum unchanged, forcing the nonrelativistic spin-up and spin-down spectra to coincide. We show that nonrelativistic spin degeneracy can coexist with relativistic spin splitting in a compensated one-dimensional magnet. In a Lieb-based construction, confinement along the diagonal cancels the projected $d$-wave spin splitting while preserving the real-space sublattice-exchange motif. Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) then locks spin to the lattice, so the Néel-vector orientation selects a magnetic line group that can reveal spin-split bands. Using fully compensated $[110]$ Ta$_2$TeSeO nanoribbons as a prototype, we find spin-degenerate nonrelativistic bands and sizable SOC splitting in the inherited easy-axis domain, $\mathbf N\parallel[100]$ or $[010]$. For sufficiently wide ribbons that retain the parent easy-axis order, this splitting is an equilibrium property. The easy-axis ribbon also supports a right-moving-mode spin polarization of about $35\%$ at finite ideal conductance. Our results establish one-dimensional fully compensated altermagnetic functionality hidden inside apparently conventional antiferromagnetic bands.

AI.tldr: Under 1D confinement, a fully compensated collinear altermagnet can lose its hallmark nonrelativistic spin splitting yet retain relativistic (SOC) spin splitting, enabling hidden altermagnetic functionality in apparently conventional antiferromagnetic nanoribbons.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetism is standardly diagnosed by nonrelativistic spin-split bands in a compensated collinear magnet. This diagnostic can fail under one-dimensional confinement, where a boundary-compatible sublattice-exchange operation may leave the sole Bloch momentum invariant, forcing nonrelativistic spin-up and spin-down spectra to coincide—potentially hiding altermagnetic order. The paper aims to show that such hidden altermagnetism can nonetheless manifest through relativistic spin splitting.
AI.method: The authors analyze nonrelativistic spin degeneracy versus relativistic spin splitting in a compensated 1D magnet. Using a Lieb-based construction, they show that confinement along the diagonal cancels the projected d-wave spin splitting while preserving the real-space sublattice-exchange motif. Spin-orbit coupling then locks spin to the lattice, so the Néel-vector orientation selects a magnetic line group that can reveal spin-split bands. They use fully compensated [110] Ta2TeSeO nanoribbons as a prototype, computing band structures for easy-axis domains (N ∥ [100] or [010]) and evaluating transport spin polarization.
AI.result: The [110] Ta2TeSeO nanoribbons exhibit spin-degenerate nonrelativistic bands together with sizable SOC-induced spin splitting in the inherited easy-axis domain (N ∥ [100] or [010]). For sufficiently wide ribbons retaining the parent easy-axis order, this splitting is an equilibrium property. The easy-axis ribbon also supports a right-moving-mode spin polarization of about 35% at finite ideal conductance.
AI.conclusion: Nonrelativistic spin degeneracy can coexist with relativistic spin splitting in a compensated 1D magnet, establishing one-dimensional fully compensated altermagnetic functionality that is hidden inside apparently conventional antiferromagnetic bands.

title: Interplay of spin-lattice and electronic coupling far above Neel ordering in 2D antiferromagnetic CrPS4 and its interface manifestation
summary: A short-range spin correlation driven, strongly intercoupled spin-phonon-electronic state far above TN (~38K) is identified in the low dimensional van der Waals antiferromagnet CrPS4. Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy reveals spin-phonon coupling persisting up to T*~120K, concomitant with local lattice distortion. The setting of vibronic progression in photoluminescence spectra suggests the strengthening of electron-phonon coupling around T*. Furthermore, both the electrical transport and optoelectronic response also change significantly at T*. The results indicate that spin-phonon coupling above TN in CrPS4 originates from local lattice distortion induced by short range magnetic correlations which in turn enhances the electron-phonon interaction. Furthermore, using a CrPS4/In2Se3 heterostructure, we demonstrate that the anomaly associated with the coupled degrees of freedom in CrPS4 also influences the adjacent In2Se3 layer. The lattice dynamics of In2Se3 is significantly modified across the magnetic anomaly of CrPS4, and the coupled dynamics is observed at T*. These interfacial manifestation opens up new possibilities for achieving correlated multifunctionalities in artificially designed heterostructure.

AI.tldr: A strongly intercoupled spin-phonon-electronic state persists far above the Néel temperature (~38 K) in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrPS4, driven by short-range spin correlations, and this coupled anomaly can be transferred to an adjacent In2Se3 layer in a heterostructure.
AI.motivation: Conventional understanding ties coupled spin-phonon-electronic phenomena to long-range magnetic order below the ordering temperature (TN). The authors aim to show that short-range spin correlations alone can drive a strongly coupled state well above TN in a low-dimensional van der Waals magnet, and to explore whether such coupled degrees of freedom can be extended across an interface into a neighboring material.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy, photoluminescence spectroscopy (vibronic progression analysis), electrical transport measurements, and optoelectronic response measurements were performed on the low-dimensional van der Waals antiferromagnet CrPS4. A CrPS4/In2Se3 heterostructure was fabricated, and the lattice dynamics of the In2Se3 layer were probed across the magnetic anomaly of CrPS4.
AI.result: Spin-phonon coupling in CrPS4 persists up to T* ~ 120 K (far above TN ~ 38 K), accompanied by local lattice distortion. Vibronic progression in the photoluminescence spectra indicates strengthened electron-phonon coupling around T*. Electrical transport and optoelectronic response also change significantly at T*. In the CrPS4/In2Se3 heterostructure, the lattice dynamics of In2Se3 are significantly modified across the magnetic anomaly of CrPS4, with coupled dynamics observed at T*.
AI.conclusion: Short-range magnetic correlations in CrPS4 induce local lattice distortion, which in turn enhances electron-phonon interaction, producing a strongly intercoupled spin-phonon-electronic state far above TN. title: Acoustic Wave-Function Imaging of Sublattice Physics in a Kagome Lattice
summary: The canonical kagome band structure hosts a Dirac cone, saddle-point van Hove singularities (vHS), and a flat band. Characteristically, these features exhibit distinct sublattice localization within the three-site basis of the kagome lattice. However, experimental proof of this sublattice character is challenging and requires direct access to both the real-space wave function and its associated momentum-space texture. Here, we implement an acoustic kagome lattice on the cm scale and measure the full excitation spectrum, thereby imaging the wave function at each lattice site, including both amplitude and phase. This enables investigation of the momentum-dependent sublattice texture across the complete band structure, particularly at the flat band and at the mixed- and pure-sublattice van Hove singularities. Our results are in excellent agreement with minimal tight-binding model calculations and constitutes the first direct experimental observation of the sublattice-resolved band structure in a kagome lattice.

AI.tldr: An acoustic kagome lattice reveals the full momentum- and sublattice-resolved band structure, directly confirming Dirac cone, van Hove singularities, and flat band sublattice textures.
AI.motivation: The kagome band structure features a Dirac cone, van Hove singularities, and a flat band with distinct sublattice localization, but experimental proof of this sublattice character requires direct access to both the real-space wave function and its momentum-space texture, which has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors implement a cm-scale acoustic kagome lattice and measure the full excitation spectrum, imaging the wave function at each lattice site with both amplitude and phase.
AI.result: Momentum-dependent sublattice texture is resolved across the complete band structure, particularly at the flat band and mixed- and pure-sublattice van Hove singularities, agreeing excellently with minimal tight-binding model calculations.
AI.conclusion: This constitutes the first direct experimental observation of the sublattice-resolved band structure in a kagome lattice.

title: Bridging steady-state and time-domain descriptions of molecular electron transport
summary: Electron transmission from an input electrode, through a molecular system, to an output electrode has been widely studied using the steady-state non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) method. Recently, the wave packet method, which provides access to the transient dynamics of electrons as well as internal molecular degrees of freedom, has been employed to investigate enantiospecific electron transport through chiral molecules. In this work, we derive the quantitative relation between the transmission of a finite-size wave packet and the energy-resolved NEGF transmission, showing that the former corresponds to a spectral average of the latter weighted by the wave packet energy distribution. Exploiting this correspondence, we construct non-Gaussian auxiliary wave packets whose spectral weight encodes the Landauer energy-window, allowing current-voltage characteristics to be obtained directly from time propagation. We further show that the correspondence extends to spin-resolved transport in a spin-phonon model of chirality-induced spin selectivity.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact correspondence between finite-size wave packet transmission and the energy-resolved NEGF transmission, showing the former is a spectral average of the latter weighted by the wave packet's energy distribution, enabling direct computation of current-voltage characteristics from time propagation.
AI.motivation: Steady-state NEGF is the standard tool for electron transmission through molecular junctions, but it does not give transient dynamics or internal molecular degrees of freedom. The wave packet method captures these, yet its relation to established NEGF transmission quantities has remained unclear, hampering interpretation and cross-validation.
AI.method: Derive analytically the quantitative relation between finite-size wave packet transmission and energy-resolved NEGF transmission, establishing the wave packet transmission as a weighted spectral average. Then design non-Gaussian auxiliary wave packets whose spectral weight is engineered to match the Landauer energy window, so that I-V characteristics follow directly from time propagation. Extend the correspondence to spin-resolved transport in a spin-phonon model of chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS).
AI.result: A formal correspondence is established: wave packet transmission equals a wave-packet-energy-weighted average of the NEGF transmission. Non-Gaussian auxiliary packets encoding the Landauer window yield I-V curves directly from time propagation. The mapping also holds for spin-resolved transport in the spin-phonon CISS model.
AI.conclusion: The wave packet and NEGF pictures are unified, providing a rigorous bridge that lets transient wave packet simulations reproduce steady-state transport observables such as I-V characteristics, and extending to spin-resolved CISS transport.

title: Correlation enhanced altermagnetism mediated by spin-lattice coupling in CrSb
summary: Altermagnets (AMs) exhibit momentum-dependent spin splitting without net magnetization, making them promising platforms for spintronic applications. While the symmetry and multipolar origins of nonrelativistic altermagnetic spin splitting (NRASS) are well established, the role of electronic correlations and spin-lattice coupling (SLC) in controlling NRASS remain unexplored. In particular, SLC provides a direct pathway for tuning altermagnetism through lattice degrees of freedom. Here we first investigate the role of electronic correlations on altermagnetic strength in NiAs-type material CrSb using density functional theory (DFT), DFT+$U$, and dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). We find that increasing electronic correlations substantially enhance NRASS and drive the stabilization of an incommensurate spin-spiral (SS) state, while dynamical correlations further amplify the spin splitting through quasiparticle renormalization of the Cr-$3d$ states. We find that the NRASS remains 12.5\% larger in DFT+DMFT than in DFT. By evaluating SLC in next step, we establish its direct connection to the evolution of NRASS and identify SLC as a microscopic descriptor between electronic correlation and enhanced altermagnetism in CrSb. Investigating it in another NiAs-type compound MnTe, we show that the SLC-NRASS correlation is generic across AMs and establish SLC as a microscopic descriptor of altermagnetic strength. Our results provide a unified framework for tuning altermagnetism through the interplay between the electronic correlations and lattice degrees of freedom.

AI.motivation: Momentum-dependent spin splitting without net magnetization makes altermagnets promising for spintronics. Symmetry and multipolar origins of nonrelativistic altermagnetic spin splitting (NRASS) are established, but the roles of electronic correlations and spin-lattice coupling (SLC) in controlling NRASS remain unexplored. SLC offers a direct route to tune altermagnetism via lattice degrees of freedom.
AI.method: DFT, DFT+U, and DFT+DMFT calculations on NiAs-type CrSb to assess electronic correlations; evaluation of spin-lattice coupling and its link to NRASS evolution; extension to NiAs-type MnTe to test generality.
AI.result: Increasing correlations substantially enhance NRASS and stabilize an incommensurate spin-spiral state; dynamical correlations further amplify splitting via quasiparticle renormalization of Cr-3d states, with NRASS 12.5% larger in DFT+DMFT than DFT. SLC connects directly to NRASS evolution, and the SLC-NRASS correlation is generic across AMs (CrSb, MnTe).
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified framework for tuning altermagnetism through the interplay of electronic correlations and lattice degrees of freedom, establishing SLC as a microscopic descriptor of altermagnetic strength.

title: Unraveling the Kagome Antiferromagnetic $3J$ Model and Its Materials: An Integrated Approach
summary: We investigate the ground-state and finite-temperature properties of the kagome antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model with three inequivalent couplings, dubbed the 3J model, which is designed for the candidate Dirac quantum spin liquid (QSL) material YCu$_3$(OH)$_6$Br$_2$[Br$_{1-x}$(OH)$_x$] (see, e.g., Zeng et al., 2024). Employing large-scale density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) supplemented by neural quantum states (NQS) simulations, we identify an intermediate QSL phase between two magnetically ordered phases. We also find that this QSL is separated from the kagome spin liquid ground state at the isotropic limit. To establish a direct comparison with experiments, we compute the specific heat of the model by means of advanced exponential (XTRG) and tangent-space (tanTRG) thermal tensor-network methods. In the magnetically ordered phase, the specific heat over temperature exhibits a shoulder at a temperature that is a fraction of the coupling strength $J_{hex}$, which disappears in the QSL phase. These universal behaviors are consistent with the experimentally observed specific heat in 3J materials for both ordered and QSL candidate samples. Our work thus connects microscopic models with experimentally measurable signatures, exemplifying an integrated approach (see Meng et al., 2026) to understanding QSL phenomena in frustrated quantum magnets, with 3J materials serving as a representative case and providing a foundation for future studies.

AI.tldr: The authors study a 3-coupling kagome antiferromagnetic Heisenberg (3J) model for the candidate Dirac quantum spin liquid material YCu3(OH)6Br2[Br1-x(OH)x], combining large-scale DMRG and neural quantum states to map its phase diagram, and thermal tensor-network methods (XTRG, tanTRG) to compute specific heat for direct experimental comparison.
AI.motivation: The 3J kagome material family is a promising platform for Dirac quantum spin liquids, but a microscopic model connecting its couplings to experimentally measurable thermodynamic signatures is needed. Understanding whether a genuine QSL phase exists in this anisotropic (three-inequivalent-coupling) regime, and how it relates to the isotropic kagome spin liquid, is an open question.
AI.method: Large-scale density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) supplemented by neural quantum states (NQS) simulations to determine the ground-state phase diagram; advanced exponential thermal tensor-network renormalization (XTRG) and tangent-space TRG (tanTRG) to compute finite-temperature specific heat.

AI.conclusion: The 3J microscopic model reproduces experimentally observed specific-heat signatures, linking model parameters to measurable quantities. This exemplifies an integrated theoretical-experimental approach to QSL physics in frustrated quantum magnets, with 3J materials as a representative case and a foundation for future work.

title: Interplay of Kekulé order, flat bands and electron-phonon coupling in graphene
summary: The Kekulé order in graphene is known to give rise to extended flat bands near the van Hove singularity (VHS) and enhanced electron-phonon coupling. However, the microscopic mechanism underlying the coexistence of these effects remains unclear. Here, it is shown that they jointly emerge as a consequence of the lattice distortion manifested through the differentiation of carbon bonds and associated electronic hoppings. In this picture, the conduction band around the $M$ point decreases almost linearly in width with increasing Kekulé order, while the VHS and dimensionless electron-phonon coupling exhibit approximately quadratic upward responses. The resulting enhancement of the electron-phonon coupling is governed predominantly by the increasing density of states at the VHS, with the effective deformation potential remaining weakly affected by the distortion. As such, the obtained results are consistent with previous related theoretical and experimental studies, while also pointing toward a potential shallowing of the conduction band under the characteristic $1/4$ filling and an increasing relevance of nonadiabatic electron-phonon effects beyond the conventional Migdal approximation. Altogether, these findings highlight the potential of controlled Kekulé ordering for engineering emergent correlated quantum phases in graphene.

AI.tldr: Kekulé ordering in graphene simultaneously flattens the conduction band and enhances electron-phonon coupling, both driven by bond differentiation and the resulting density of states at the van Hove singularity.
AI.motivation: Extended flat bands near the van Hove singularity (VHS) and enhanced electron-phonon coupling coexist in Kekulé-ordered graphene, but the microscopic mechanism linking these two effects is unclear. The paper aims to explain their common origin.
AI.method: The authors model the Kekulé distortion via differentiation of carbon bonds and the associated electronic hoppings, then track how the conduction band near the M point, the VHS, and the dimensionless electron-phonon coupling respond quantitatively to increasing Kekulé order.
AI.result: The conduction band width near the M point decreases almost linearly with increasing Kekulé order, whereas the VHS and dimensionless electron-phonon coupling show approximately quadratic upward responses. The coupling enhancement is governed predominantly by the rising density of states at the VHS, while the effective deformation potential is only weakly affected by the distortion.

title: Anisotropy of Ultrafast Strain in $V_2O_3$ Thin Films: Out-of-Equilibrium Phase Transitions under Interfacial Clamping
summary: Ultrafast photoinduced insulator-to-metal transitions in correlated materials are often mediated by lattice distortions, yet the role of interfacial lattice constraints in shaping nonequilibrium pathways remains largely unexplored. We use azimuth-resolved time-resolved X-ray diffraction to track orientation-dependent strain dynamics in granular V$_2$O$_3$ thin films on c-cut sapphire, where thermal-expansion mismatch imposes anisotropic interfacial strain. Across the thermal transition, the azimuthal profile of the (110)$_H$ strain inverts curvature, providing direct evidence of partial clamping of the hexagonal basal-plane lattice (a$_H$,b$_H$). After photoexcitation of the antiferromagnetic insulating phase, the structural response remains clamp-limited: weakly constrained grain families reach the full basal-plane contraction characteristic of the metallic-like state, whereas strongly constrained families exhibit a strongly reduced distortion. Fluence-dependent measurements further disentangle transformed fraction from clamping-limited lattice distortion. Our results show that interfacial clamping acts as a static selector for ultrafast phase switching and provide a general route to quantify anisotropic strain dynamics in heterostructures.

AI.tldr: Interfacial lattice clamping in V₂O₃ thin films on sapphire acts as a static selector that limits the ultrafast photoinduced insulator-to-metal lattice response, with weakly constrained grains fully contracting while strongly constrained grains are suppressed.
AI.motivation: Photoinduced insulator-to-metal transitions in correlated materials are usually attributed to lattice distortions, but how interfacial lattice constraints shape these nonequilibrium pathways is largely unexplored. This work addresses the role of anisotropic interfacial strain imposed by thermal-expansion mismatch in heterostructures.
AI.method: Azimuth-resolved time-resolved X-ray diffraction was used to track orientation-dependent strain dynamics in granular V₂O₃ thin films grown on c-cut sapphire, probing the azimuthal profile of the (110)_H strain across the thermal transition and after photoexcitation of the antiferromagnetic insulating phase, complemented by fluence-dependent measurements.
AI.result: The azimuthal profile of the (110)_H strain inverts curvature across the thermal transition, evidencing partial clamping of the hexagonal basal-plane lattice (a_H, b_H). After photoexcitation, weakly constrained grain families reach the full basal-plane contraction of the metallic-like state, while strongly constrained families show strongly reduced distortion; fluence-dependent measurements separate transformed fraction from clamping-limited lattice distortion.
AI.conclusion: Interfacial clamping functions as a static selector for ultrafast phase switching and offers a general route to quantify anisotropic strain dynamics in heterostructures.

title: Learning Quantum Matter through Attention in Complex Space
summary: Magnetic many-electron wavefunctions require amplitude and phase to be optimized together. Whether a complex internal representation improves this variational search is a practical question for neural wavefunction design. We introduce Complex Psiformer for interacting electrons in a magnetic moiré continuum, combining complex hidden features and Hermitian-magnitude attention with magnetic boundary conditions and fermionic antisymmetry. After the same number of optimization steps, Complex Psiformer reaches lower energies than Real Psiformer in two finite supercells. Both Psiformers also improve on their respective neural Hartree-Fock references. Across five training seeds in the 25-cell system, the mean Complex advantage is 1.458 meV per electron, with a smaller observed spread. A separately trained two-electron Complex state has a smaller energy gap to a finite configuration interaction reference than its Real counterpart. In the Complex states, flux scans show nonmonotonic density correlations and weaker honeycomb mean-density modulation at higher flux, while connected fluctuations persist. Gauge invariant current maps provide a qualitative comparison of local circulation in the optimized states. These benchmarks support the combined architecture as a variational ansatz for studying energies and charge arrangements in finite magnetic systems.

AI.tldr: Complex Psiformer, a neural wavefunction with complex hidden features and Hermitian-magnitude attention, outperforms Real Psiformer in energy and gap benchmarks for interacting electrons in a magnetic moiré continuum, while also revealing flux-dependent correlation and current structure.
AI.motivation: Magnetic many-electron wavefunctions need amplitude and phase optimized jointly. It is practically unclear whether a complex internal representation improves the variational search, motivating a direct comparison of complex versus real neural wavefunction designs under magnetic boundary conditions and fermionic antisymmetry.
AI.method: The authors introduce Complex Psiformer for interacting electrons in a magnetic moiré continuum. It combines complex hidden features and Hermitian-magnitude attention with magnetic boundary conditions and fermionic antisymmetry. They compare it against Real Psiformer at equal optimization steps in two finite supercells, train across five seeds in a 25-cell system, train a separate two-electron state against a finite configuration interaction reference, and perform flux scans plus gauge-invariant current maps.

Across five training seeds in the 25-cell system, the mean Complex advantage is 1.458 meV per electron with smaller spread.
